questions.question: Do you work or are you a student?
questions.model_answer: Well, I am currently a university student studying economics. To be honest, it keeps me quite busy, but I genuinely enjoy it because it helps me make sense of the world around us. I also do some part-time tutoring on the side, so it is a nice balance.

questions.question: Why did you choose that job / field of study?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, I chose this field because I have always had a strong passion for technology and problem-solving. And I think another reason was that it offers a wide range of career prospects, which mattered a lot to me. Having grown up in a family of engineers probably played a role in it as well.

questions.question: What do you like / dislike about your job?
questions.model_answer: What I enjoy most is probably the variety — no two days are really the same. I also get a real sense of satisfaction when a project comes together. On the other hand, the workload during peak periods can feel quite overwhelming sometimes.

questions.question: What do you like / dislike about your studies?
questions.model_answer: I'd say the best part is the practical projects — when you can apply what you've learned to real situations, everything clicks into place. That said, the sheer volume of coursework can feel hard to manage at times. I've come to accept that as part of the process, though.

questions.question: What was your dream job when you were young?
questions.model_answer: Funnily enough, I wanted to be a pilot — I was absolutely captivated by the idea of flying. I used to spend hours reading about aircraft and airports. Most kids go through that phase, don't they? But obviously my interests took a different direction as I grew up.

questions.question: Have you changed your mind on your dream job?
questions.model_answer: Definitely. My ambitions have shifted quite significantly over the years. Back then, I was convinced I would follow a creative path, whereas now I am far more drawn to technology and education. I think life experience and the people you meet play a huge role in shaping your direction.

questions.question: Please describe your hometown a little.
questions.model_answer: I am from Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan. It is quite a large, bustling metropolis with a rich blend of modern architecture and historical landmarks. What I love most about it is how it strikes a balance between tradition and modernity — ancient mosques sit right alongside contemporary glass buildings.

questions.question: Do you like your hometown?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I have a deep affection for it — it is where I grew up and where most of my fondest memories are. That said, the traffic can be quite hectic, and the summers are honestly brutally hot. But overall, the warmth of the people and the culture more than make up for those things.

questions.question: Is that a big city or a small place?
questions.model_answer: It is definitely a big city — Tashkent is one of the largest cities in Central Asia, in fact. In terms of population, it has grown considerably over the past few decades. So while it can feel a bit overwhelming at times, it also means there is always a great deal going on — festivals, events, restaurants — which I genuinely enjoy.

questions.question: What colour would you choose to paint the walls of your room?
questions.model_answer: I think I'd go with something like a muted sage green or a warm off-white — colours that promote a sense of calm. I find that neutral tones tend to make a room feel larger and more inviting.

questions.question: What colour would you never use in your home?
questions.model_answer: I'd have to say a very bright, harsh neon colour — like a vivid orange or a fluorescent yellow. I just think they create visual noise and can be quite overwhelming to live with on a daily basis. I've always believed that a home should be a relaxing retreat, not a place that overstimulates the senses.

questions.question: Can you describe the place where you live?
questions.model_answer: I live in a fairly spacious apartment in the residential part of the city. What I particularly like is that we have a small park nearby, so I can clear my head whenever I need to. It's somewhere I've grown very attached to over time.

questions.question: What do you like about your flat?
questions.model_answer: What I love most is probably the natural light — we have large windows, and the apartment gets flooded with sunlight throughout the day, which really lifts the mood. Apart from that, I love how cosy and well-organised it is — it truly feels like a sanctuary after a long day.

questions.question: What can you see from the windows where you live?
questions.model_answer: From my window, I can see a tree-lined street below and, in the distance, a cluster of apartment blocks. It's not exactly the most scenic view, but I do enjoy watching the street come to life in the morning — people going about their routines, children heading to school. It gives the place a kind of lived-in energy that I find comforting.

questions.question: Do you take photos of buildings?
questions.model_answer: Yes, actually — I quite enjoy it. Particularly when I travel, I find myself drawn to interesting architecture — things like ornate facades or the play of light and shadow on a building's surface. I think photography is a great way to capture the character of a place, and buildings say a great deal about the culture and history of a city.

questions.question: Is there a building that you would like to visit?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely. I've always wanted to visit the Sagrada Família in Barcelona — it's one of those architectural masterpieces that you see in photos and struggle to believe is real. What fascinates me is how it has been under construction for over a century and yet still pushes the boundaries of design and engineering.

questions.question: What did you enjoy doing as a child?
questions.model_answer: Well, if I'm being honest, I was completely obsessed with drawing and building things. I used to spend hours just sitting at the kitchen table with coloured pencils, making up cartoon characters and little maps. Apart from that, I loved being outdoors — climbing trees, exploring the neighbourhood with friends. Looking back, I think what made it so enjoyable was the complete absence of pressure — you just did things because they made you happy.

questions.question: Did you enjoy your childhood?
questions.model_answer: Yes, genuinely, I did. It was not perfect — no childhood ever is — but I have really fond memories of it. What I remember most is a sense of freedom that I do not think adults ever quite recapture. That said, there were difficult moments too. But overall, I think I was fortunate to grow up in an environment where I felt safe and cared for. I've come to appreciate that more as I have got older.

questions.question: Do you remember your dreams when you wake up?
questions.model_answer: Sometimes, yes, but it really depends on the night. If the dream is particularly vivid or emotionally intense, I tend to hold onto it for a while. But most of the time, the details fade remarkably quickly — by the time I have made my morning coffee, it is usually all but gone.

questions.question: Do you think dreams will affect life?
questions.model_answer: I think they can, at least on a subconscious level. Sometimes I wake up feeling strangely unsettled or motivated, and that mood carries into my day. That said, I do not personally put too much weight on specific dream content — I see them more as a window into what is already preoccupying my mind rather than any kind of prediction.

questions.question: Do you think dreams have special meanings?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, I am on the fence about that. Some cultures place huge importance on dream interpretation, and I find that fascinating. Personally, I think dreams can sometimes reveal something about your emotional state — things you are worried about or haven't fully processed. But whether they carry a specific symbolic meaning that can be decoded — I'd say I am more sceptical about that.

questions.question: Do you like hearing other people's dreams?
questions.model_answer: It depends, actually. If it is short and genuinely bizarre or funny, then yes — there is something oddly entertaining about it. But if someone goes into very long detail, I will be honest — my attention tends to wander a bit. I've noticed that other people's dreams are usually far more interesting to the person telling them than to the listener.

questions.question: Do you share your dreams with others?
questions.model_answer: Occasionally, yes — mostly with close friends or family. If I have had a particularly strange or vivid dream, I will sometimes mention it over breakfast. But I try not to go on about it for too long — I'm aware that what feels significant and meaningful in the moment often sounds rather mundane when put into words.

questions.question: What kinds of food do you particularly like?
questions.model_answer: Well, I have always been a huge fan of Uzbek cuisine — there is something incredibly comforting and satisfying about a well-made plov or lagman. But I also really enjoy Japanese food — the way it is beautifully balanced in terms of flavour and presentation. In general, I tend to prefer food that is flavourful but not overly heavy.

questions.question: What kinds of food are most popular in your country?
questions.model_answer: In Uzbekistan, plov is really the undisputed king of our cuisine — it is deeply embedded in our culture and served at almost every celebration. Apart from that, dishes like samsa, shashlik, and dimlama are incredibly well-loved. What's interesting is that Uzbek food has a strong communal aspect — it is traditionally meant to be shared with family and guests.

questions.question: Is there any food you don't like?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, yes — I find very pungent or fermented foods quite difficult. Things like strong blue cheese or certain pickled fish are just not for me at all. I think it mainly comes down to texture and smell rather than taste itself. That said, I try not to be too fussy about food — I have learned to appreciate things I did not like as a child, which suggests my palate is still developing.

questions.question: What kind of gifts are popular in your country?
questions.model_answer: In Uzbekistan, I would say practical gifts are very popular — things like quality fabrics, homewares, or food items like dried fruits and sweets. For celebrations like weddings or Navruz, people often give cash gifts as well, which is completely socially acceptable here. More recently, I have noticed younger people gravitating towards more personalised or experience-based gifts, which reflects a gradual cultural shift.

questions.question: What's the best gift you have ever received?
questions.model_answer: That's a lovely question to think about. I think the best gift I ever received was a handwritten journal from my closest friend on my birthday. What made it special was that she had filled the first pages with memories and quotes from our friendship — it was completely unexpected and deeply personal. I genuinely believe that thoughtful, personal gifts always outweigh anything expensive but impersonal.

questions.question: What do you give others as gifts?
questions.model_answer: It really depends on the person, honestly. For close friends, I try to choose something tailored to their interests — a book I know they would love, or something connected to a hobby of theirs. For more general occasions, I usually go with something practical and high-quality. I put a lot of thought into gifts because I think a poorly chosen gift can feel almost worse than no gift at all.

questions.question: What gift have you received recently?
questions.model_answer: Actually, just last month my colleague gave me a beautiful handcrafted notebook as a thank-you for helping her with a project. At first I thought it was quite simple, but I have genuinely come to love it — I use it every day for notes and ideas. It is funny how a small, thoughtful gesture can stay with you so much longer than something expensive.

questions.question: How do we choose gifts?
questions.model_answer: I think the key is really knowing the person well enough to understand what would genuinely add value to their life. Personally, I try to think about what they are currently interested in, what they might need, or what they would never buy for themselves. I've found that the best gifts often reflect a conversation you have had with someone — they show that you were actually listening.

questions.question: Is there anything that has made you feel happy lately?
questions.model_answer: Actually, yes — just last week I finished a book I had been putting off for a while, and it was incredibly uplifting. The warmer weather has also been lifting my spirits lately. I think it is often the small, everyday things — a good conversation, a nice cup of tea, a walk in fresh air — that bring the most genuine joy.

questions.question: What made you happy when you were little?
questions.model_answer: Oh, definitely spending time with my family — particularly weekends at my grandparents' house, where there was always food, laughter, and a wonderful sense of warmth and togetherness. I also used to be really passionate about drawing, and I could lose myself in it for hours. Looking back, I think what made childhood happiness so pure and uncomplicated was that you were happy simply because you were doing something you loved.

questions.question: What do you think will make you feel happy in the future?
questions.model_answer: I think in the long run, what will make me genuinely happy is having a sense of purpose — feeling that my work actually makes a difference to people. Beyond that, I hope to have meaningful relationships and enough time to pursue the things I care about. I genuinely believe that happiness is not a destination you reach but more of a way of engaging with everyday life — finding contentment in small things rather than waiting for some big moment.

questions.question: How do people remember each stage of their lives?
questions.model_answer: I think people tend to remember life stages through key milestones — things like starting school, first relationships, or significant challenges they overcame. Sensory triggers like a familiar smell or a particular song can also instantly transport you back to a specific time. In my experience, the moments that carry the strongest emotional weight — whether joyful or painful — are the ones that stick most vividly in the memory.

questions.question: At what age do you think people are the happiest?
questions.model_answer: That is genuinely a difficult question to answer. Personally, I feel most content now, in my twenties, because I have enough independence to make my own choices but still feel full of possibilities. However, many people say their childhood years were the happiest, before the weight of responsibility set in. I think happiness is actually less about age and more about the quality of your relationships and your sense of purpose.

questions.question: Do you enjoy being the age you are now?
questions.model_answer: Yes, genuinely. I feel like I am at an exciting stage of life — there is a real sense of freedom and possibility that I did not fully appreciate when I was younger. Of course, it comes with its own pressures — finances, career choices, figuring out who you are. But overall, I would not trade this stage for any other. I think every age has something to offer if you approach it with the right mindset.

questions.question: What did you often do with your friends in your childhood?
questions.model_answer: We used to spend most of our time outdoors — cycling around the neighbourhood, playing football, exploring places we probably should not have. There was also a lot of just hanging around together with no particular plan, which sounds dull but was actually genuinely enjoyable. I think the simplicity was part of what made it so good — we did not need organised entertainment, just each other's company and enough space to be ourselves.

questions.question: Do you have any plans for the next five years?
questions.model_answer: Yes, definitely. In the short term, I am focused on completing my studies and getting some solid professional experience. Beyond that, I would love to further my education — possibly do a postgraduate degree at some point. I try to have a clear direction without being too rigid about the specific path.

questions.question: What do you think is the most important thing at the moment?
questions.model_answer: Personally, I think the most important thing right now is maintaining good mental health. The world feels incredibly fast-paced and demanding, and there is a great deal of pressure on young people from social media, career expectations, and uncertainty about the future. So I think taking care of your wellbeing and nurturing genuine human connections has never been more important.

questions.question: Are you good at memorising things?
questions.model_answer: I would say I am reasonably good at it, particularly for things I find genuinely interesting. I tend to remember facts, conversations, and ideas from areas I care about quite easily. However, I really struggle with phone numbers, dates, or repetitive administrative information — my memory does not seem to retain things it finds mundane. I think most people are selectively good at memory based on what they are emotionally invested in.

questions.question: Have you ever forgotten something important?
questions.model_answer: Yes, embarrassingly so. Once I completely forgot about an important presentation at university because I had been so caught up in other assignments that it just slipped my mind entirely. It was genuinely mortifying and very stressful. Since then I have been much more diligent about keeping a planner and setting reminders for anything time-sensitive. It was a painful lesson but a genuinely useful one.

questions.question: How do you remember important things?
questions.model_answer: These days, I rely heavily on technology — I use my phone calendar and reminder apps to keep track of deadlines and commitments. But for studying, I have found that active recall — testing yourself rather than just re-reading — is far more effective at actually retaining information. Writing things down by hand also seems to cement things in my memory better than typing, which I think says something about how physical engagement strengthens memory.

questions.question: Do you like to get up early?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, not naturally — I am definitely more of a night owl than an early bird. But I have been making a conscious effort to wake up earlier recently because I genuinely notice that I am far more productive in the mornings when I actually manage it. That said, it is still a real struggle most days — I think I have reluctantly accepted that being an early riser is a skill I need to build rather than a trait I was born with.

questions.question: What is your morning routine?
questions.model_answer: On weekdays, I try to keep it fairly structured. I wake up, have a glass of water, make coffee — that part is completely non-negotiable — and then spend about fifteen minutes looking through my tasks for the day. If I have enough time, I will go for a short walk before starting work, which I find really sharpens my focus. I have learned that how I start the morning tends to set the tone for everything that follows.

questions.question: What do you usually do in the morning?
questions.model_answer: During the week, I follow a fairly fixed routine — breakfast, a quick check of my messages, and then I start whatever needs doing. On weekends, though, I let myself be much more relaxed — I sleep in a little, make a proper breakfast rather than just grabbing something quickly, and ease into the day at a much slower pace. Those relaxed weekend mornings are honestly one of my favourite parts of the week.

questions.question: What loud noise can you hear where you live?
questions.model_answer: Well, I live near a fairly busy road, so traffic noise is pretty much a constant throughout the day — particularly during rush hour. There also seems to be ongoing construction nearby, which has been going on for months and can be quite disruptive when I am trying to concentrate. It quiets down considerably at night, which I am genuinely grateful for.

questions.question: Would you like to live in a less noisy place?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely. Noise is something that really affects my concentration and general sense of wellbeing, probably more than most people. Ideally, I would love to live somewhere with more greenery around — perhaps a quieter residential neighbourhood. I think there is something genuinely restorative about being in a place where you can actually hear yourself think.

questions.question: Do you enjoy listening to loud music?
questions.model_answer: It really depends on the situation. When I am exercising or need a burst of energy before something demanding, loud, upbeat music can be genuinely energising. But in general, I prefer music at a moderate volume — loud enough to enjoy but not so overwhelming that it blocks out everything else. I tend to think of music more as a backdrop to what I am doing rather than something to be consumed at full volume.

questions.question: What's your favourite animal?
questions.model_answer: If I had to choose, I would say dogs — I have always had a real soft spot for them. I think it is because of their loyalty and the genuine emotional connection they form with people. There is something really special about the bond between a dog and its owner that is hard to replicate with any other animal. They are also endlessly entertaining to be around.

questions.question: Have you ever had a pet?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I had a cat growing up. She was incredibly independent — very typical of cats, I suppose — but also surprisingly affectionate when she wanted to be. Looking back, I cherish those memories quite a lot. She was a constant presence throughout my childhood, and having her taught me a great deal about responsibility and empathy.

questions.question: What's the most popular animal in your country?
questions.model_answer: I would say dogs are probably the most common household pet in Uzbekistan, though cats have been growing in popularity too, especially among younger city dwellers. Beyond pets, horses hold a very special place in our culture — they are deeply embedded in Uzbek history and tradition, and you still see them celebrated at national events and cultural festivals. There is a real reverence for horses that goes beyond simply seeing them as working animals.

questions.question: Would you like to see more public places near where you live?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely. I think our neighbourhood could really benefit from more well-maintained public spaces — parks, squares, places where people can gather and unwind. At the moment, there are very few spots nearby where you can simply sit and escape the noise of the city. I think access to good public spaces makes a real difference to daily quality of life.

questions.question: Do you often go to public places with your friends?
questions.model_answer: I would say moderately often. During warmer months, we tend to meet up in parks or along the waterfront — it is a low-cost and genuinely enjoyable way to spend time together. That said, in colder months we tend to gravitate towards cafés. But overall, public spaces are very much a regular part of our social life.

questions.question: Why do people like to go to parks?
questions.model_answer: I think there are a few key reasons. Most obviously, parks offer a rare connection to nature in an otherwise concrete environment. There is strong evidence that this significantly reduces stress. Beyond that, parks are also democratic spaces — free, welcoming, with no expectation to buy anything.

questions.question: Do you like to take pictures of good scenery?
questions.model_answer: Yes, very much. There is something satisfying about capturing a view that genuinely takes your breath away. I find that trying to frame a scene well makes you slow down and actually look more carefully. I think photography is a great way to stay present in a beautiful place.

questions.question: Do you prefer urban or rural scenery?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, I find myself drawn to both for different reasons. Urban scenery has its own visual energy. But when I need to genuinely recharge, I always find myself gravitating towards open landscapes. So if I had to choose, I would probably say rural — but it would be a close call.

questions.question: Do you prefer the mountains or the sea?
questions.model_answer: The mountains, I think. There is something deeply calming about being surrounded by peaks — the sense of scale and permanence makes everyday problems feel temporarily insignificant. That said, the sea has its own hypnotic quality.

questions.question: Have you ever been part of a sports team?
questions.model_answer: Yes, actually — I played for a local basketball team at school. Looking back, it was one of the most formative experiences of that period. It taught me a lot about discipline, communication, and resilience — particularly how to bounce back after a loss. The social side was just as valuable — the bonds you build through training tend to be very strong.

questions.question: Do you prefer team sports or individual sports?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, I prefer team sports, mainly because of the shared sense of achievement. When you succeed as a team, the joy is amplified because it belongs to everyone. That said, I can absolutely see the appeal of individual sports — the complete personal accountability can be intensely clarifying.

questions.question: Are team sports popular in your country?
questions.model_answer: Yes, very much so. Football is by far the most popular team sport. What's interesting is that sport here is very much a community affair — watching and supporting brings people together in a way few other activities can. National competitions in particular inspire a real sense of collective pride.

questions.question: Do you use technology a lot in your daily life?
questions.model_answer: Yes, quite a lot — probably more than I stop to reflect on. I use my phone constantly for communication and staying informed, and my laptop for work and study. Technology has become so seamlessly integrated into everyday life that it is almost invisible. That said, I do try to be intentional about when and how I use it.

questions.question: What kinds of technology do you use most?
questions.model_answer: In terms of frequency, my smartphone is probably the device I interact with most frequently. Beyond that, I rely heavily on my laptop for studying, writing, and research-heavy tasks. I also use cloud storage services heavily, which has transformed how I manage my files. I think the most useful technology is the kind that runs quietly in the background.

questions.question: How often do you use a computer?
questions.model_answer: Pretty much every day, without exception. For my studies alone, I spend several hours on my laptop daily. Outside of studying, I also use it for creative projects and keeping in touch with people. Honestly, there are days when I feel I have been staring at a screen far too long and I make a conscious effort to step away from it in the evenings.

questions.question: Do you type on a desktop or laptop keyboard every day?
questions.model_answer: Yes, every single day. The vast majority of my work happens on a laptop. In fact, I would find it hard to estimate how many hours I type per day — probably more than I care to admit. It has become second nature to the point where I rarely think about it anymore.

questions.question: When did you learn how to type on a keyboard?
questions.model_answer: I think I was around ten or eleven. At first I used to type with just two fingers. Over time, I just picked it up naturally through practice — nobody formally taught me. I remember being genuinely proud the first time I typed without looking at the keys. It is one of those skills you never truly appreciate until you imagine not having it.

questions.question: How do you improve your typing?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, most of my improvement has come from sheer volume of practice. That said, I have occasionally used online speed and accuracy tools to identify where I make the most errors. I think the most effective approach is deliberate, focused practice rather than mindlessly repeating the same movements.

questions.question: Would you like to be a teacher?
questions.model_answer: I have thought about this quite seriously. On one hand, I find the idea of nurturing someone's understanding genuinely exciting. On the other hand, teaching requires enormous patience and emotional stamina. So in short, the honest answer is: possibly, but only in the right context.

questions.question: Do you think you could be a teacher?
questions.model_answer: I think I have some of the qualities it requires — I communicate reasonably well and I genuinely enjoy breaking complex things down. That said, I think patience is genuinely my biggest challenge — I can sometimes project those expectations onto others. It is something I would need to work on.

questions.question: Did you have a favourite teacher?
questions.model_answer: Yes, definitely — my English teacher at secondary school. What made her different was that she never treated the class as a passive audience — she always made us think critically and argue our points. She was also genuinely passionate about the subject, which was completely contagious. She planted a lasting love of language in me.

questions.question: How does this teacher help you?
questions.model_answer: Even now, I find myself drawing on what she taught me. She helped me develop a real love of reading and think more carefully about language. More broadly, she modelled what genuine intellectual curiosity looks like, which has influenced how I approach every subject since.

questions.question: How has your favourite teacher helped you?
questions.model_answer: In so many ways, but most fundamentally, she changed how I see my own potential. Before her class, I had never really thought of myself as a strong communicator. She consistently pushed me to express my ideas more clearly and never settled for a mediocre answer. Her influence on my academic confidence was absolutely decisive.

questions.question: Do you think you spend too much time on social media?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, yes — probably. If I am being completely candid, I underestimate my own usage significantly. There are evenings when I pick up my phone and find half an hour has gone by without my noticing. The platforms are deliberately designed to be addictive, which makes self-regulation genuinely difficult.

questions.question: What do people often do on social media?
questions.model_answer: From what I observe, people use social media for a wide range of purposes. Most obviously, people use it to keep up with friends and family. Beyond that, short video content consumes an enormous amount of people's attention. There is also a growing trend of using platforms to build personal brands and generate income.

questions.question: What was your dream when you were a child?
questions.model_answer: Funnily enough, I wanted to be an explorer — in the classic, somewhat unrealistic sense. I was absolutely fascinated by maps and ancient civilisations. I used to spend hours drawing imaginary maps. Looking back, I think that dream reflected a genuine curiosity about the world that has never entirely left me.

questions.question: Are you the kind of person who sticks to dreams?
questions.model_answer: I would say I am moderately tenacious. I tend to stick to goals that feel genuinely aligned with who I am. That said, I have learned that flexibility matters as much as dogged persistence — knowing when to pivot is as valuable as knowing how to keep going.

questions.question: Do you think you are an ambitious person?
questions.model_answer: In some respects, yes — though my ambitions are more personal than conventionally career-oriented. I have a strong drive to continuously improve and to make a meaningful contribution. I think it really depends on how you define ambition.

questions.question: Are you an ambitious person?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I believe so, though perhaps not in the most conventional sense of the word. I set high standards for myself and genuinely care about the quality of what I produce. At the same time, I have learned to balance drive with self-compassion — pushing myself without burning out.

questions.question: Would you use mirrors to decorate your room?
questions.model_answer: Yes, actually. I think mirrors are one of the most underrated decorative tools. What I particularly like about them is that they create an illusion of space and amplify natural light. A well-placed mirror can completely transform the feel of a room without any major renovation.

questions.question: Do you usually take a mirror with you?
questions.model_answer: Not a full mirror, no — but I always have a small compact mirror with me for convenience. It is one of those items you barely register until you need it. Beyond the practical side, I do not particularly make a habit of carrying one — I prefer not to be too self-conscious about my appearance throughout the day.

questions.question: How often do you use a mirror?
questions.model_answer: Fairly regularly throughout the day — mainly in the morning and briefly before any important event. Beyond that, I try not to check my reflection excessively — it can sometimes amplify insecurities. I think there is a healthy balance between caring about appearance and being preoccupied with it.

questions.question: Do you like looking at yourself in a mirror?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, not excessively. I think I have a reasonably healthy relationship with mirrors. I use them functionally — to check that I am presentable — rather than scrutinising my appearance. There is something psychologically interesting about the relationship people have with their reflection — it reveals quite a lot about self-image and confidence.

questions.question: Have you ever bought a mirror?
questions.model_answer: Yes, once — when I moved into my first flat. I had never really thought about how much thought goes into choosing one until I was actually in the shop. There are so many considerations — size, shape, frame style, whether the glass is true or distorts your reflection. In the end, I chose something understated that would not dominate the room.

questions.question: Do you use a mirror before buying clothing?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely — I would never buy clothes without checking how they look and fit in person. What I find interesting is how different something can look on a hanger versus on your body. Fitting room lighting and mirror quality can also be deceptively flattering, so I try to assess critically.

questions.question: What functions does a mirror have?
questions.model_answer: Well, the most obvious is the practical one — checking your appearance. Beyond that, in interior design, mirrors are used to create depth and brightness. There is also a psychological dimension — mirrors are used in therapeutic settings and in practices like mindfulness and self-reflection.

questions.question: Do you think a mirror is a good decoration?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I genuinely do. I think mirrors are among the most versatile decorative objects available. Unlike most decorative items, a mirror serves both an aesthetic and a functional purpose. What I particularly appreciate is that mirrors complement almost any interior style — whether minimalist or ornate. And unlike art, a mirror requires no particular taste to appreciate.

questions.question: Do you prefer sad or happy music?
questions.model_answer: It genuinely depends on my mood. When I am in high spirits, upbeat music amplifies that energy in a really satisfying way. But when I am feeling reflective, I prefer melancholic music — there is something deeply cathartic about it.

questions.question: Does happy music make you feel more excited?
questions.model_answer: Yes, quite noticeably. The right upbeat track can completely shift my energy level within seconds. I think music has a uniquely direct effect on our emotional state — it bypasses conscious thought. I personally use music quite deliberately — curating playlists for exercising, studying, or winding down in the evening.

questions.question: Would you say you are a tidy person?
questions.model_answer: I would say reasonably so, yes — though I was definitely more chaotic as a student. These days, I find that an organised environment directly affects my ability to concentrate. So I think tidiness is less a personality trait and more a deliberate habit I have built because it makes me more productive.

questions.question: Do you like to keep things tidy?
questions.model_answer: Yes, genuinely — though more about function than aesthetics. A tidy space means I can find things easily and transition between tasks cleanly. That said, I am not obsessively neat — some areas are deliberately left more relaxed.

questions.question: How do you keep things tidy?
questions.model_answer: I have found that small, consistent habits work far better than occasional major decluttering sessions. For example, I always reset my workspace at the end of each day. I also try to follow the rule of tidying immediately rather than letting it pile up. The key is lowering the barrier to action — making the tidy option the easy one.

questions.question: Do you think it is possible for people to be tidy all the time?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, probably not. Life is inherently messy — cooking, creativity, raising children — all naturally produce temporary disorder. I think the more psychologically healthy goal is to build systems that make restoring order quick and effortless, rather than trying to prevent all disorder.

questions.question: What kinds of websites do you often visit?
questions.model_answer: In terms of frequency, news and information sites are probably at the top — I check current affairs most mornings. Beyond that, I visit academic databases for my studies and productivity platforms to stay organised. I try to be intentional about my browsing habits and avoid websites that simply consume time without purpose.

questions.question: What kinds of websites are popular in your country?
questions.model_answer: From what I can observe, social media platforms are probably the most widely used. YouTube and Instagram have a massive following across all age groups. Beyond social media, e-commerce platforms have been growing rapidly as more people embrace online shopping. There is also a strong appetite for local content.

questions.question: What is your favourite website?
questions.model_answer: That's a good question — it changes depending on context. But if I had to pick one, I would say Wikipedia. I know that sounds unexciting, but it is one of the most democratically accessible repositories of knowledge ever created. You can fall down a rabbit hole for hours on any topic. And unlike most websites, it is ad-free and non-commercial, which feels increasingly rare.

questions.question: Are there any changes to the websites you often visit?
questions.model_answer: Yes, quite a few — mostly in design and how content is surfaced and organised. Many sites have moved towards algorithm-driven content feeds, which I have mixed feelings about. On one hand, personalisation makes discovery easier. On the other hand, it can create an information bubble that reinforces existing views.

questions.question: Do you like to wear watches?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I do — I have worn one since I was quite young. For me, it is about more than telling the time. A watch feels like a considered accessory that says something about your personality and your attention to detail. I also find it calming to check a watch rather than reaching for my phone and getting pulled into notifications.

questions.question: Do you think a watch is important for you?
questions.model_answer: Important might be a slight overstatement, but yes — it is something I genuinely value. Practically, having a watch means I am not constantly reaching for my phone, which helps me stay more present in conversations. Beyond the practical dimension, my current watch was a gift, which gives it a sentimental value that goes well beyond its function.

questions.question: Have you ever received a watch as a gift?
questions.model_answer: Yes, actually — the watch I am wearing was a gift from my parents when I graduated. What made it special was the significance of the moment it marked. I think watches are particularly meaningful gifts because they are functional and lasting — unlike flowers, they remain with you for years and accumulate meaning over time.

questions.question: Why do people like expensive watches?
questions.model_answer: I think the reasons are more layered than they might appear. On one level, expensive watches are genuinely precision-crafted instruments — the craftsmanship is remarkable, and people appreciate something built to last. But beyond craftsmanship, there is undeniably a social signalling element — expensive watches communicate wealth, taste, and success in a very subtle and lasting way.

questions.question: Do you like shopping?
questions.model_answer: It depends what for. Grocery shopping and browsing for books I genuinely enjoy. But shopping for clothes or electronics can feel overwhelming — too many options and decision fatigue can make it more stressful than enjoyable. I think I prefer purposeful shopping over aimless browsing.

questions.question: How often do you go shopping?
questions.model_answer: For everyday essentials like food, probably three or four times a week. For other things, like clothing or household items, it is much less frequent — probably once every few weeks at most, and only when I have a specific need. I find that shopping without a purpose tends to lead to impulse purchases that I later regret.

questions.question: Do you compare prices when you shop?
questions.model_answer: Yes, almost always for anything of any significant value. I think it is just good financial sense. That said, I try not to take it to extremes — if the difference is tiny, it is not worth spending significant time hunting for marginal savings.

questions.question: Is it difficult for you to make choices when you shop?
questions.model_answer: For some categories, yes. For high-involvement purchases like electronics, I can spend a considerable amount of time deliberating — sometimes to the point of paralysis. I think this is related to a strong aversion to regret. For everyday items, though, I can usually decide on the spot.

questions.question: What type of car do you like?
questions.model_answer: If I'm being honest, I have never been particularly car-obsessed, but if I had to choose I would go for something compact and fuel-efficient. That said, if cost were no concern I would be drawn to something with clean, understated design that prioritises quality over showiness.

questions.question: What colour car would you choose to buy?
questions.model_answer: Probably something in a neutral or muted tone — a dark grey or deep navy blue, probably. There are practical reasons — neutral colours hold their value better and show dirt less obviously. But honestly, I simply find garish colours quite visually jarring.

questions.question: Do you think car colours are important?
questions.model_answer: To some extent, yes. From a purely practical standpoint, colour affects visibility on the road, resale value, and interior heat. Socially, colours carry connotations of status or personality — a bright red sports car and a silver family saloon communicate very different things about their owner.

questions.question: What do you usually do when there's a traffic jam?
questions.model_answer: It depends on how bad it is. If I am a passenger I often catch up on messages or listen to a podcast. If I am alone, traffic jams are actually surprisingly good for listening to long podcasts — there is nothing else demanding your attention. That said, if I am running late for something important, it can be genuinely stressful regardless of any strategy.

questions.question: Do you prefer to be a driver or a passenger?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, a passenger — quite decisively. As a passenger I can look at the surroundings, read, or let my thoughts wander. Driving requires sustained concentration that leaves me mentally drained after any significant journey. That said, I do appreciate the independence and flexibility that being a driver provides.

questions.question: Do you like to go to parks?
questions.model_answer: Yes, quite a lot — especially when the weather is good. For me, parks serve a very specific function that nothing else in a city quite replaces — they offer a genuine escape from the density of urban life without having to leave the city. I find that even a short walk through a green space can noticeably shift my mood and energy level quite significantly.

questions.question: When was the last time you went to the park?
questions.model_answer: Actually, fairly recently — I was there just last weekend. I tend to go most weekends when the weather permits. I find it a good way to decompress after a busy week — there is something restorative about being outdoors that indoor spaces simply cannot replicate. I think regular time in nature is genuinely underrated as a simple, accessible wellbeing habit.

questions.question: Do people in your country often go to parks?
questions.model_answer: I would say yes, though it varies by city and generation. In urban centres where green space is limited, parks are heavily frequented — particularly at weekends. From what I observe, there has been a noticeable shift in recent years — parks are increasingly used for fitness and social events rather than passive leisure. This has been especially true since the pandemic.

questions.question: Do you like science?
questions.model_answer: Yes, broadly speaking — though my interest tends to be more in the big conceptual questions than in the technical detail. I am particularly drawn to physics and cosmology — questions about the origins and structure of the universe feel genuinely humbling and endlessly fascinating.

questions.question: Did you like science classes when you were young?
questions.model_answer: It was mixed, honestly. I used to find biology and earth science genuinely engaging because they connected to the observable world around me. However, chemistry and advanced physics felt abstract and disconnected — mostly because the teaching rarely contextualised the content. I think science education often underestimates the importance of curiosity.

questions.question: Do you want to travel in outer space?
questions.model_answer: Part of me does, absolutely — the idea is extraordinary and deeply compelling. But the rational side of me is acutely aware of the extraordinary physical demands and risks involved. The psychological isolation alone would be incredibly challenging. That said, if it were truly safe and commercially accessible, I genuinely think I would.

questions.question: What would you do if you had an opportunity to travel in space?
questions.model_answer: I think the very first thing would be to simply look back at the Earth. Every astronaut who has done so describes it as profoundly transformative — a moment that permanently alters your sense of perspective. Beyond that, I would want to document the experience as thoroughly as possible — writing, photographing, trying to preserve every detail of something so fleeting and extraordinary.

questions.question: Do you think it's necessary to see other planets?
questions.model_answer: I think 'necessary' is a strong word, but I do think it is scientifically and strategically important. On a scientific level, studying other planets provides crucial context for understanding our own. On a broader level, with humanity facing increasing existential risks from climate change and other sources, the capacity to establish a presence on other worlds may become genuinely critical for our survival.

questions.question: Are you interested in films about outer space and stars?
questions.model_answer: Yes, very much so — they are among my favourite films. What I find particularly compelling about the best ones is when they balance scientific accuracy with emotional depth. Films like Interstellar or The Martian are fascinating because they engage with real scientific ideas while also telling deeply human stories. I think the best science fiction is really philosophy in disguise.

questions.question: Do you like science fiction movies?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I enjoy them a lot — particularly the ones that take the science seriously. What draws me to the genre is how it uses imagined futures to reflect on present realities. The best science fiction films are not really about the future — they use it as a lens to examine who we are now. I also appreciate that the genre encourages genuine intellectual curiosity about some of the biggest questions humans can ask.

questions.question: Have you ever taken a course about stars?
questions.model_answer: Not a formal course, no — but I have done a fair amount of self-directed reading and watching on the subject. I have always been fascinated by astronomy and cosmology as topics. I think informal, passion-driven learning can sometimes be just as enriching as a formal course — perhaps more so, because you follow your curiosity rather than a fixed syllabus.

questions.question: Is it important to study stars?
questions.model_answer: I genuinely believe so, for several reasons. Most fundamentally, astronomy has been the engine of some of the most transformative scientific discoveries in human history — from understanding gravitational forces to detecting black holes. Beyond the science, there is a profound philosophical value in contemplating our place in the cosmos.

questions.question: Do you want to know more about outer space?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely — the more I learn, the more I realise how vast and complex the subject is. There are questions that genuinely captivate me — whether dark matter really exists, whether there is intelligent life elsewhere in the universe, what preceded the Big Bang. I think the universe is the most humbling and endlessly generative subject there is.

questions.question: Do you use headphones?
questions.model_answer: Yes, quite regularly — pretty much every day. For me, headphones have become one of the most genuinely indispensable pieces of technology I own. I use them for listening to music, podcasts, and online lectures — basically anything where I need to focus without disturbing others. I think good headphones are one of the best investments for sustained focus and mental wellbeing.

questions.question: In what situations would you use headphones?
questions.model_answer: In quite a few different situations, actually. Most commonly, I use them when I am doing focused, deep work — they help me block out environmental distraction. I also use them when commuting or travelling, which turns otherwise dead time into something useful. And occasionally, I use them simply to signal to others that I am not available.

questions.question: What type of headphones do you use?
questions.model_answer: At the moment, I use two different types depending on the context. At home, I prefer over-ear headphones because the sound quality and noise isolation are significantly better. When I am out and about, I use wireless earbuds because they are far more practical for movement. I think the sign of really good headphones is when the audio feels completely natural and immersive.

questions.question: In what situations would you NOT use headphones?
questions.model_answer: There are quite a few, actually. Most obviously, I would never use them while cycling or driving — the safety implications are serious and impossible to ignore. Beyond that, in any social setting where I am expected to be fully present — meals, conversations, meetings — headphones would be disrespectful and disengaging.

questions.question: Do you think singing can bring happiness to people?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I genuinely believe so — and there is strong scientific evidence to support it. Singing triggers the release of endorphins and oxytocin — chemicals associated with pleasure and social bonding. Beyond the biology, there is something deeply expressive about the act of singing that allows people to release emotions they cannot easily articulate in words alone. I think this is why singing exists in virtually every culture throughout human history.

questions.question: Did you like singing when you were a child?
questions.model_answer: Very much so — I sang almost constantly, which I imagine drove my family to distraction. Looking back, I think children sing so naturally and freely because they have not yet developed self-consciousness. I think one of the quietly sad things about growing up is that self-consciousness gradually replaces spontaneity.

questions.question: Do you often sing now?
questions.model_answer: Not as openly as I once did — self-consciousness has definitely taken hold. That said, I do still sing — just in private, uninhibited contexts like the shower or in the car. I think most adults gradually lose the freedom to sing publicly as social inhibitions increase. It is one of the areas where I genuinely envy children their unselfconsciousness.

questions.question: Do you think you are a tidy person?
questions.model_answer: I would say so, yes — though I have become significantly tidier as I have got older. When I was a student, my living space was fairly chaotic by most standards. Now, I find that a disorganised environment genuinely affects my ability to think clearly. So I think neatness is less about natural instinct and more a deliberately cultivated habit I have built because it directly supports my focus.

questions.question: Do you keep your room or workspace tidy?
questions.model_answer: I try to, yes — my workspace more consistently than my living space. For me, a clear desk is less an aesthetic preference and more a functional necessity. When my workspace is cluttered, I find it difficult to maintain sustained focus. So I have developed a simple routine of resetting my space at the end of every day so each morning starts with a clean slate.

questions.question: Is it important for your study or work environment to be neat?
questions.model_answer: Yes, very much so — I notice a very direct correlation between the state of my environment and the quality of my work. When my space is orderly and clutter-free, my concentration is noticeably sharper. I think this is because physical disorder creates cognitive noise that competes with your work. That said, I recognise it is at least partly a personal predisposition — some people genuinely work well in a more fluid, energetic environment.

questions.question: What is your favourite advertisement?
questions.model_answer: There is one particular advert that has always stuck with me — it was for a well-known sports brand and featured an incredibly moving narrative about perseverance. What made it memorable was not the product itself but the emotional story it told. I think the best advertisements are the ones that tell a genuine story rather than simply listing features.

questions.question: Why do you think some adverts are memorable?
questions.model_answer: I think memorability usually comes down to emotional resonance or humour. Advertisements that make us feel something — whether that is joy, nostalgia, or even sadness — tend to lodge themselves in our memory far more effectively than straightforward product descriptions. A clever jingle or an unexpected twist can also make an advert unforgettable.

questions.question: Do you think advertisements are reliable?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, I think you have to take most adverts with a healthy dose of scepticism. Their primary goal is to sell, which means they naturally highlight the positives and downplay any negatives. That said, reputable brands generally cannot afford to be completely misleading because the backlash from consumers and regulators would be too damaging. So I would say they are reliable to a point, but always worth fact-checking.

questions.question: Do you like watching adverts on TV or online?
questions.model_answer: It depends on the context. Online adverts can be quite intrusive, especially when they interrupt a video every few minutes, and I tend to find them frustrating. On the other hand, well-made TV commercials during a break can sometimes be genuinely entertaining. I think the key difference is that online ads often feel forced upon you, whereas TV adverts are more expected.

questions.question: What types of advertising are most common in your country?
questions.model_answer: In Uzbekistan, I would say television and social media advertising dominate. Billboards and outdoor advertising are also very visible in urban centres, particularly for mobile phone operators and car brands. In recent years, influencer marketing has grown enormously, particularly on Instagram and Telegram, which reflects a broader global trend.

questions.question: Do you enjoy celebrating your birthday?
questions.model_answer: To be honest, I have mixed feelings about it. On one hand, it is lovely to spend time with friends and family and feel appreciated. On the other hand, as I have got older, I sometimes feel a bit self-conscious about being the centre of attention. These days I prefer smaller, more intimate gatherings rather than big parties.

questions.question: What is the most important age in your country?
questions.model_answer: I think the age of eighteen is particularly significant in Uzbekistan because that is when people are legally considered adults. It marks the transition to full legal rights and responsibilities. Beyond that, I think sixteen is also quite important because that is when many young people take their first major independent steps in education and social life.

questions.question: How do you feel about getting older?
questions.model_answer: I think I have come to accept it with a degree of serenity. There is something genuinely comforting about gaining life experience and feeling more settled in who you are. That said, I do sometimes miss the boundless energy and optimism of being very young. I think the key is to embrace each stage for what it offers rather than mourning what has passed.

questions.question: Do you think old age can be a happy time?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely, though I think it largely depends on health, financial security, and social connections. People who maintain strong relationships and remain mentally active tend to be genuinely content in later life. In my culture, elders are deeply respected and surrounded by family, which I think contributes enormously to their happiness.

questions.question: What age did you enjoy the most?
questions.model_answer: If I had to choose, I would probably say my early twenties. I had enough independence to make my own decisions but was still young enough to feel that the future was wide open. It was a period of real personal growth — discovering what I cared about, forming lasting friendships, and gaining confidence.

questions.question: Do you like reading books?
questions.model_answer: Yes, very much — though I have to admit I do not read as much as I would like to. When I do find the time, I genuinely lose myself in a good book. There is something irreplaceable about the depth and quiet focus that reading demands, which is quite different from watching a film or scrolling through social media.

questions.question: What kind of books do you prefer?
questions.model_answer: I tend to gravitate towards non-fiction, particularly history and psychology, because I enjoy learning about how the world and the human mind work. That said, I do occasionally read fiction, especially literary novels with well-developed characters. I think variety keeps reading fresh and engaging.

questions.question: Do you prefer reading physical books or e-books?
questions.model_answer: Physical books, without question. There is something deeply satisfying about holding a book, feeling the pages, and seeing your progress. I also find that I retain information better from paper than from a screen. E-books are convenient for travel, but for serious reading I always prefer a printed copy.

questions.question: Did you read a lot when you were a child?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I was quite a voracious reader as a child — I used to devour entire series of adventure books during the school holidays. My parents encouraged it, and we had a small but well-stocked home library. I think that early habit of reading shaped my imagination and vocabulary in ways I am still grateful for.

questions.question: Do people in your country read a lot?
questions.model_answer: I think it varies quite significantly by generation and location. Older generations, particularly those who grew up before the internet, tend to read more. Among younger people, reading has declined somewhat in favour of digital content, though there has been a small resurgence of interest in recent years.

questions.question: Do you like chatting with friends?
questions.model_answer: Yes, absolutely — it is one of the things I value most. Whether it is a deep, meaningful conversation or just light-hearted banter, I find chatting with friends genuinely restorative. I think human connection is fundamental to wellbeing, and a good conversation with someone who knows you well is hard to beat.

questions.question: Do you prefer chatting face-to-face or online?
questions.model_answer: Face-to-face, without a doubt. While online messaging is convenient, it strips away so much of the nuance — body language, tone of voice, the energy in the room. A face-to-face conversation feels more present and authentic. That said, when friends live far away, video calls are a reasonable compromise.

questions.question: What do you usually chat about with your friends?
questions.model_answer: It really depends on the friend and the mood. With some friends we talk about work, ambitions, and the challenges we are facing. With others it is more light-hearted — films, travel plans, shared memories. I think the best friendships are the ones where you can comfortably move between serious topics and complete nonsense.

questions.question: Do you think you are good at communication?
questions.model_answer: I think I am reasonably good, though I am always working on it. I have learned to listen more attentively and to ask better questions rather than simply waiting for my turn to speak. That said, I can sometimes overthink before speaking, which means I am not always as spontaneous as I would like to be.

questions.question: Is public speaking difficult for you?
questions.model_answer: It used to be genuinely terrifying for me. However, after doing several presentations at university, I have become much more comfortable. I think preparation is everything — when I know my material well, the nerves diminish significantly. That said, I still feel a flutter of adrenaline before any big presentation.

questions.question: What kind of clothes do you like to wear?
questions.model_answer: I tend to gravitate towards comfortable, understated clothing — well-fitted jeans, simple shirts, and good-quality knitwear. I value quality over quantity, so I prefer to invest in a few versatile pieces that last rather than following every trend. Comfort is definitely a priority for me.

questions.question: Do you prefer casual or formal clothes?
questions.model_answer: Casual, almost always. I find formal clothes can feel a bit restrictive and performative, whereas casual wear allows me to move freely and feel like myself. That said, I do appreciate the sense of occasion that comes with dressing up for a special event — it is just not something I would choose for everyday life.

questions.question: Do you like shopping for clothes?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, I find it a bit stressful. Too many options and the artificial lighting in changing rooms do not help. I prefer to shop with a clear idea of what I need rather than browsing aimlessly. Online shopping has made it easier, though sizing can be unpredictable.

questions.question: What colours do you like to wear?
questions.model_answer: I mostly wear neutral tones — navy, grey, white, and olive green. I find them easy to mix and match, and they tend to age well. Occasionally I will wear a muted burgundy or mustard if I want something with a bit more personality, but I generally avoid anything too bright or flashy.

questions.question: Are clothes important to you?
questions.model_answer: To a moderate extent, yes. I do not think clothes define a person, but they do affect how you feel and how you are perceived. Wearing something well-made and comfortable gives me a quiet confidence. That said, I would never judge someone based on what they are wearing — character matters far more than fashion.

questions.question: Do you like watching films?
questions.model_answer: Yes, very much — it is probably my favourite form of entertainment. There is something uniquely immersive about cinema that no other medium quite replicates. A truly great film can make you see the world differently, even if only for a couple of hours.

questions.question: What kind of films do you like?
questions.model_answer: I tend to enjoy films that balance entertainment with substance — psychological thrillers, well-crafted dramas, and the occasional science fiction film that explores big ideas. I am less interested in pure action or superhero films, though I can enjoy them in the right mood. What I value most is a strong script and believable characters.

questions.question: Do you prefer watching films at home or at the cinema?
questions.model_answer: For big, visually ambitious films, the cinema is unbeatable — the scale of the screen and the surround sound create an experience you simply cannot replicate at home. But for quieter, dialogue-driven films, I actually prefer watching at home where I can pause, reflect, and really absorb what is being said.

questions.question: How often do you go to the cinema?
questions.model_answer: Not as often as I would like, unfortunately — probably once every couple of months. Life gets busy, and it is easy to put off going. But whenever I do make the effort, I am always glad I did. There is something special about the shared experience of watching a film with a crowd of strangers.

questions.question: Who is your favourite actor or actress?
questions.model_answer: That is a difficult question because there are so many talented performers. If I had to choose one, I would probably say Meryl Streep, simply because of her extraordinary range and consistency over such a long career. The way she inhabits completely different characters is genuinely remarkable.

questions.question: Do you have a lot of friends?
questions.model_answer: I would not say a lot, no — I tend to value depth over breadth. I have a small circle of close friends who I have known for years, and I find that far more fulfilling than having dozens of acquaintances. Quality of connection matters far more to me than quantity.

questions.question: What do you usually do with your friends?
questions.model_answer: It varies depending on the friend and the season. In warmer months we often meet in parks or cafés, sometimes for a walk along the river. In colder weather, we tend to gather at someone's flat for a home-cooked meal and conversation. Board games have also become a surprisingly regular feature of our get-togethers.

questions.question: How do you make new friends?
questions.model_answer: I think shared interests are the most reliable foundation — whether that is a class, a sport, or a mutual friend who introduces you. I am not someone who finds it easy to strike up conversations with complete strangers, but when there is a common activity or context, I find it much more natural.

questions.question: Do you think friendship is important?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely — I think it is one of the most important things in life. Good friends provide emotional support, honest feedback, and a sense of belonging that is hard to find elsewhere. Research consistently shows that strong social connections are one of the biggest predictors of long-term happiness and even physical health.

questions.question: What qualities do you look for in a friend?
questions.model_answer: Honesty and reliability are probably at the top of my list. I value friends who are genuinely there for you during difficult times, not just when things are going well. A good sense of humour helps too — the ability to laugh together, even at yourselves, is a wonderful bond.

questions.question: Do you exercise regularly?
questions.model_answer: I try to, though I would not say I am perfectly consistent. I generally manage three or four sessions a week — a mix of jogging, swimming, and some light strength training at home. I have noticed that when I exercise regularly, my mood and concentration improve noticeably, so I make it a priority even when I am busy.

questions.question: What kind of exercise do you like?
questions.model_answer: I have always enjoyed swimming the most — there is something deeply meditative about being in the water, and it is gentle on the joints while still giving you a full-body workout. I also enjoy jogging outdoors, particularly early in the morning when the streets are quiet and the air is fresh.

questions.question: Do you think it is important to be healthy?
questions.model_answer: Without question. Good health is the foundation upon which everything else is built — your work, your relationships, your ability to enjoy life. I have seen how illness can completely derail someone's plans and ambitions, and it has made me deeply appreciative of the importance of looking after yourself.

questions.question: How do you stay healthy?
questions.model_answer: I focus on a few core habits: regular exercise, plenty of sleep, and eating a balanced diet with lots of vegetables and minimal processed food. I also try to manage stress by making time for relaxation and social connection. It is not always perfect, but consistency matters more than perfection.

questions.question: Do young people in your country exercise enough?
questions.model_answer: Honestly, I think many do not. Between academic pressures and the allure of screens, physical activity often takes a back seat. That said, there has been a growing fitness culture among young people in recent years — gyms, yoga studios, and running clubs have become quite popular in urban areas.

questions.question: How often do you use the internet?
questions.model_answer: Pretty much every day, without exception. I use it for work, communication, entertainment, and staying informed about current events. It has become so woven into modern life that a day without it feels genuinely unusual. That said, I do try to set boundaries so I am not constantly glued to a screen.

questions.question: What do you use the internet for?
questions.model_answer: A bit of everything, honestly — studying, messaging friends, watching films, reading news, and occasionally online shopping. The internet is such a versatile tool that it is hard to think of an area of life it does not touch in some way. I think its greatest strength is the instant access to information.

questions.question: Do you think children should use the internet?
questions.model_answer: I think they should, but with clear boundaries and supervision. The internet is an incredible educational resource, and children who grow up digitally literate will have a significant advantage. However, there are genuine risks — inappropriate content, online predators, and the addictive design of many platforms. So parental guidance is absolutely essential.

questions.question: Do you prefer shopping online or in physical stores?
questions.model_answer: It depends on what I am buying. For books, electronics, and items where specifications matter, I prefer online because comparison is easier. But for clothes and shoes, I still prefer physical stores because fit and fabric quality are impossible to judge from a photo. I think the ideal is a blend of both.

questions.question: What are the disadvantages of the internet?
questions.model_answer: There are quite a few. The most significant is probably the erosion of attention spans — the constant stream of notifications and short-form content makes deep focus increasingly difficult. There is also the issue of misinformation, cyberbullying, and the way social media can amplify anxiety and comparison. It is a powerful tool, but one that requires conscious, disciplined use.

questions.question: What languages do you speak?
questions.model_answer: I speak Uzbek and Russian fluently, and I am currently working on my English. I also know a few basic phrases in Korean because I have been fascinated by the culture for a while. I have always believed that each language you learn opens up a completely new way of seeing the world.

questions.question: Do you think it is important to learn foreign languages?
questions.model_answer: Absolutely — I think it is one of the most valuable skills a person can develop. Beyond the obvious practical benefits for travel and work, learning a language deepens your understanding of different cultures and ways of thinking. It also enhances cognitive abilities like problem-solving and multitasking.

questions.question: What is the most difficult thing about learning a language?
questions.model_answer: For me, the hardest part has always been mastering natural pronunciation and intonation. Grammar and vocabulary can be learned through study, but sounding like a native speaker requires years of immersion and careful listening. Another challenge is overcoming the fear of making mistakes in front of others.

questions.question: How do you practise speaking English?
questions.model_answer: I try to weave it into my daily life as much as possible. I watch English-language films without subtitles, listen to podcasts, and I have a language exchange partner who I speak with twice a week. I also make a point of thinking in English sometimes, which I think helps internalise the grammar patterns.

questions.question: Will you learn another language in the future?
questions.model_answer: I would love to. I have been thinking about learning either Spanish or Mandarin — both are incredibly useful and open up huge cultural worlds. Spanish feels more immediately accessible because of its phonetic spelling, but Mandarin would be a fascinating intellectual challenge. I think I will probably start with Spanish.

questions.question: Do you like travelling?
questions.model_answer: Very much so — it is one of my greatest passions. There is something genuinely transformative about stepping outside your everyday environment and experiencing a different culture, cuisine, and way of life. Even short trips can shift your perspective in unexpected ways.

questions.question: What kind of places do you like to visit?
questions.model_answer: I am drawn to cities with rich history and character — places where you can feel the layers of time in the architecture and the streets. That said, I also deeply appreciate natural landscapes, particularly mountains and coastlines. I think the contrast between urban energy and natural calm keeps my travels balanced.

questions.question: Have you travelled to many foreign countries?
questions.model_answer: A few, but not as many as I would like. So far I have visited Turkey, Russia, and South Korea. Each one left a lasting impression on me, and I have a long list of places I still want to see. I think travel is one of those things where the more you do it, the more you realise how much is still out there.

questions.question: Do you prefer to travel alone or with others?
questions.model_answer: It depends on the trip. For city breaks and cultural exploration, I prefer company because sharing discoveries makes them more meaningful. But for longer, more reflective journeys — particularly hikes or retreats — I sometimes prefer to be alone. Solitary travel forces you to rely on yourself in a way that is very growth-oriented.

questions.question: What is the most important thing when planning a trip?
questions.model_answer: I think flexibility is the most underrated quality in travel planning. Having a rough itinerary is useful, but being open to unexpected opportunities — a local festival, a recommendation from a stranger — often leads to the most memorable experiences. Beyond that, good travel insurance and a basic grasp of local customs are essential.

questions.question: What is the weather like in your country?
questions.model_answer: Uzbekistan has quite an extreme continental climate — brutally hot summers with temperatures well over forty degrees, and very cold winters that can drop below minus ten. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons, with mild temperatures and clear skies. The contrast between seasons is really quite dramatic.

questions.question: What is your favourite season?
questions.model_answer: Spring, without question. After the long, grey winter, the arrival of blossoms and warmer days feels genuinely rejuvenating. There is a particular energy in the air — people seem more optimistic, and outdoor cafés begin to fill up again. It is the season of renewal, and I find that very appealing.

questions.question: Do you prefer hot or cold weather?
questions.model_answer: I would say I prefer cooler weather, though extremes of either are unpleasant. Hot weather can be exhausting, particularly when combined with high humidity. Cold weather, on the other hand, can be invigorating if you are dressed appropriately, and there is something deeply comforting about being warm indoors while it is freezing outside.

questions.question: Does the weather affect your mood?
questions.model_answer: Definitely. I find that overcast, rainy days tend to make me feel more subdued and introspective, whereas bright, sunny days lift my energy and motivation. It is a well-documented phenomenon — lack of sunlight can genuinely affect serotonin levels. I have learned to accept the quieter mood of grey days rather than fighting it.

questions.question: What do you usually do when the weather is bad?
questions.model_answer: I tend to turn inwards — reading, watching films, cooking something comforting, or catching up on indoor tasks I have been putting off. I also find that bad weather is a good excuse to slow down and rest, which is something I often neglect when the sun is shining and the world feels demanding.

questions.question: Do you write by hand often?
