questions.model_answer: Far less than I used to, unfortunately. Most of my writing is done on a laptop or phone — emails, messages, notes. I only really write by hand when taking quick notes in a meeting or signing documents. I do miss the tactile satisfaction of pen on paper sometimes.

questions.question: Do you prefer typing or handwriting?
questions.model_answer: For anything longer than a paragraph, typing is far more efficient — it is faster, easier to edit, and the result is more legible. But for personal journaling or brainstorming, I still prefer handwriting. There is something about the physical act of writing that seems to engage different, more creative parts of the brain.

questions.question: Is your handwriting good?
questions.model_answer: It used to be quite neat when I was in school and practised regularly, but these days it has deteriorated somewhat. When I write quickly, it can become almost illegible. I have been making a conscious effort to slow down and write more carefully when I do pick up a pen.

questions.question: Do you think handwriting is still important?
questions.model_answer: I think it is less critical than it once was for practical communication, but it still carries significance. There is a personal quality to a handwritten note that an email simply cannot replicate. Some research also suggests that handwriting aids memory retention more effectively than typing. So while not essential, I do not think it should be abandoned entirely.

questions.question: Did you like writing essays at school?
questions.model_answer: It depended entirely on the topic. If it was something I cared about — history, literature, social issues — I genuinely enjoyed the process of researching and constructing an argument. But when the topic felt arbitrary or dull, it was a real struggle. I think enthusiasm for writing is largely determined by whether you feel the subject matters.

questions.question: Do you save money?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I try to, though I am not as disciplined as I would like to be. I have a monthly budget and I put a fixed amount into savings at the beginning of each month. The challenge is resisting impulse purchases — particularly online, where buying is so frictionless.

questions.question: What do you spend money on?
questions.model_answer: My biggest expenses are rent, food, and transport. Beyond the essentials, I spend a reasonable amount on books, the occasional concert or film, and eating out with friends. I also try to set aside a small amount each month for travel. I think spending on experiences tends to bring more lasting happiness than spending on objects.

questions.question: Did you get pocket money when you were a child?
questions.model_answer: Yes, a small amount — enough to buy the occasional snack or toy. My parents used it as a way to teach me the value of money and the importance of saving for something you really want rather than spending impulsively. Looking back, I think it was a valuable early lesson in financial discipline.

questions.question: Do you think money is important?
questions.model_answer: To a certain extent, yes — it provides security, freedom, and access to opportunities. However, I do not believe it is the most important thing in life. Beyond a certain threshold, additional money does not significantly increase happiness. What matters more is how you use it — on meaningful experiences, supporting others, and creating a life aligned with your values.

questions.question: Do young people in your country save money?
questions.model_answer: I think it varies. Some young people are quite financially aware and start saving early, particularly those with clear goals like further education or buying a home. But many find it difficult to save because living costs are high and there is a strong culture of immediate gratification through consumer spending. I think financial education could make a real difference.

questions.question: Do you like parties?
questions.model_answer: It depends on the kind of party. Small gatherings with close friends, where you can actually talk and connect, I genuinely enjoy. But large, noisy parties with people I do not know well tend to drain me. I think I am more of an introvert in that sense — quality of interaction matters far more than quantity.

questions.question: What kind of parties do you like?
questions.model_answer: I prefer dinner parties or board game evenings — something where there is a shared activity and conversation flows naturally. Outdoor barbecues in summer are also wonderful. What I dislike are parties where the music is so loud that you cannot hear yourself think, let alone have a proper conversation.

questions.question: Do you prefer to throw a party or attend one?
questions.model_answer: Attend, almost certainly. Throwing a party involves an enormous amount of planning, shopping, cooking, and cleaning up afterwards. I find the stress of hosting tends to outweigh the enjoyment. When I attend someone else's party, I can simply relax, socialise, and enjoy myself without any of the logistical burden.

questions.question: What do people usually do at parties in your country?
questions.model_answer: It varies by occasion. For birthdays and weddings, there is usually a big meal, toasts, music, and dancing. For more casual get-togethers, people might simply chat, play games, or watch a film together. One lovely tradition in Uzbek culture is that guests always bring something — food, sweets, or flowers — as a gesture of appreciation.

questions.question: Have you ever had a surprise party?
questions.model_answer: Yes, once — for my twenty-first birthday. My friends had planned it meticulously, and I was completely taken aback when I walked into the room and everyone shouted 'Surprise!' I remember feeling a genuine rush of emotion — gratitude, shock, and happiness all at once. It was one of the most memorable evenings of my life.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a movie you watched and enjoyed recently
bullets: When and where you watched it
And explain why you enjoyed this movie
part2.model_answer: ⏱ Approx. 2 minutes at natural speaking paceWell, the film that immediately springs to mind is Interstellar, which I had been meaning to watch for quite some time. I ended up watching it at home with my older brother a few months ago — we both cleared our schedules for it, which tells you how much we were looking forward to it.The film is a science fiction epic about astronauts who travel through a wormhole in search of a new home for humanity. What makes it stand out, at least for me, is that it does not simply rely on spectacular visual effects — it delves into incredibly thought-provoking themes — time, sacrifice, love across impossible distances.What I found particularly moving was the relationship between the main character and his daughter — it carried an emotional weight that stayed with me long after the film ended. I genuinely believe it is one of those rare films that transcends its genre and speaks to something deeply human. I would recommend it without hesitation to anyone who enjoys both spectacle and substance.

part3_questions.question: What kinds of movies are popular in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: From what I've observed, action films and comedies are by far the most popular genres. In recent years there has also been a growing appetite for local productions, which I think reflects a broader shift in how people value their own culture.

part3_questions.question: What qualities make a good actor?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think the most essential quality is emotional authenticity — the ability to make an audience truly believe what they are feeling. Beyond that, versatility matters enormously — the capacity to inhabit completely different characters convincingly.

part3_questions.question: Is self-confidence important for actors?
part3_questions.model_answer: Absolutely — I'd argue it is absolutely indispensable. Acting requires vulnerability in front of large audiences, and without a strong sense of self, that vulnerability would be impossible to sustain over a long career.

part3_questions.question: What is the difference between watching films at the cinema and at home?
part3_questions.model_answer: The most obvious difference is the immersive quality of the cinema — the scale of the screen and the enveloping sound create an experience hard to replicate at home. On the other hand, watching at home offers a level of comfort and flexibility that cinemas simply cannot match — you can pause, rewind, and watch in your own time.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a music event that you didn't enjoy
bullets: Why you decided to go there
And explain why you didn't enjoy it
part2.model_answer: ⏱ Approx. 2 minutes at natural speaking paceThe event that comes to mind is an outdoor music festival I attended about two years ago with university friends. It was a local event on the outskirts of the city, and I'll be honest, I only agreed to go because I did not want to let my friends down. The genre was heavy electronic music, which is not really my cup of tea if I am being truthful.What made it worse was the sheer size of the crowd — it was absolutely heaving, and I spent most of the evening struggling to find any personal space. The music itself was relentlessly loud, to the point where I couldn't hear myself think.Looking back, I think the experience taught me something important — that peer pressure is not a good enough reason to attend an event. From that point on, I have been much more selective about which events I attend.

part3_questions.question: Do you think people's music tastes change as they get older?
part3_questions.model_answer: I definitely think so. As people mature, they often gravitate towards music that is more emotionally nuanced. The raw energy of youth-oriented music gives way to a preference for depth and craftsmanship as people develop a deeper frame of reference for the themes being explored.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people prefer live music over recorded music?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think it comes down to the sense of shared experience — there is something profoundly connecting about experiencing music in a crowd. Recorded music, however perfect technically, can never fully replicate the spontaneity and energy of a live performance.

part3_questions.question: Do you think music events are becoming more commercialised nowadays?
part3_questions.model_answer: Without a doubt. The focus has increasingly shifted from the music itself towards the festival experience as a product. Ticket prices have skyrocketed, and major sponsors now dominate the landscape. While this brings greater production value, it can strip away the authentic spirit that made those events special.

part3_questions.question: Is it necessary for children to take music lessons?
part3_questions.model_answer: I wouldn't say necessary, but I do think it is enormously beneficial. Music education helps children develop discipline and patience, and there is compelling evidence that it enhances cognitive development. That said, forcing children into lessons against their will is likely to be counterproductive.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACE / EXPERIENCEDescribe a bicycle / motorcycle / car trip you would like to go on
bullets: Who you would like to go with
Where you would like to go
When you would like to go
And explain why you would like to go by bicycle / motorcycle
part2.model_answer: ⏱ Approx. 2 minutes at natural speaking paceWell, this is something I've actually thought about quite a lot. The trip I would love to do is a motorcycle journey through the Fergana Valley in eastern Uzbekistan. I would want to go with my two closest friends, both of whom share my passion for off-the-beaten-track destinations.In terms of timing, I would want to go in early spring, when the landscapes are at their most breathtaking — orchards in full blossom, the air still cool and crisp. I have always felt that travelling by motorcycle is simply the most authentic way to experience a landscape. You are not sealed off from your surroundings the way you are in a car — you feel the temperature change as you descend into valleys, you smell the wildflowers, you hear the countryside around you.Perhaps most importantly, I think a trip like that would be genuinely transformative — a chance to step away from the daily routine and reconnect with what actually matters.

part3_questions.question: Which form of transportation is more popular in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: I'd say private car ownership is still overwhelmingly dominant in Uzbekistan, particularly outside cities. That said, public transport in Tashkent has been improving steadily, and attitudes are gradually shifting, especially among younger generations who are more environmentally conscious.

part3_questions.question: Why do more people own and drive private vehicles nowadays?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think there are a number of factors at play. First and foremost, a private car offers unmatched convenience. Beyond that, in many cultures, car ownership is closely tied to social status — it is seen as a symbol of success and independence.

part3_questions.question: Do people need to change their transportation habits to protect the environment?
part3_questions.model_answer: Without question. The carbon footprint of private vehicles is substantial, and unless significant changes are made, the environmental consequences will be irreversible. That said, meaningful change requires not just individual willpower but investment in viable public transport alternatives.

part3_questions.question: What do you think about the future of electric cars?
part3_questions.model_answer: I'm cautiously optimistic. The technology has come a long way in a remarkably short time, and as production costs fall, electric vehicles will become increasingly accessible. However, the key challenge remains charging infrastructure — without a comprehensive network, widespread adoption will remain limited.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PERSONDescribe a child you know who likes drawing very much
bullets: How you knew him / her, what he / she is like
And explain why you think he / she likes drawing
part2.model_answer: ⏱ Approx. 2 minutes at natural speaking paceThe person who immediately comes to mind is my younger cousin, Kamron, who is eight years old. I have known him since he was born — we are an incredibly close-knit family, so I see him regularly at family gatherings and weekends.Kamron is a remarkably imaginative child — always in his own world, observing things that most people walk straight past. He draws virtually every day — whether it is at the kitchen table after school or in the margins of his exercise books.As for why he enjoys it so much, I think drawing gives him a way to externalise his inner world — the things he imagines that he cannot yet articulate in words. Beyond that, there is also an element of control — on paper he can create anything, and that sense of creative agency is something that clearly means a great deal to him.

part3_questions.question: What is the right age for a child to learn drawing?
part3_questions.model_answer: Honestly, I don't think there is a fixed answer — children begin making marks on paper as soon as they can hold a crayon, and that instinct to create should be nurtured from the very beginning. What matters more than age is providing children with the freedom to explore without judgment.

part3_questions.question: Why do most children draw more often than adults?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think the main reason is that children have not yet been conditioned to doubt themselves. Adults, on the other hand, have internalised a fear of judgment — they worry about whether the result is good enough, whereas children simply enjoy the act of creation itself.

part3_questions.question: Should schools teach art to children?
part3_questions.model_answer: Absolutely, yes. Art education does far more than simply teach drawing — it cultivates critical and creative thinking, emotional intelligence, and the ability to see the world from multiple perspectives. These are qualities that will serve them throughout their lives, regardless of the career they choose.

part3_questions.question: Do you think galleries and museums should be free of charge?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think so, yes — at least for permanent collections. Art is part of our shared cultural heritage, and access to it should not be contingent on financial means. That said, institutions still need sustainable funding models, so charging for special exhibitions seems like a reasonable compromise.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACEDescribe a city that you have been to and would like to visit again
bullets: What you did there and what it was like
And explain why you would like to visit it again
part2.model_answer: ⏱ Approx. 2 minutes at natural speaking paceThe city that immediately comes to mind is Istanbul. I had the opportunity to visit about three years ago with a group of friends, and honestly, it is a place that left a lasting impression on me in a way that few cities ever have.What struck me most was how effortlessly the city blends two continents, two histories, and two entirely different atmospheres. The old city felt steeped in centuries of history, and yet just across the Bosphorus there were modern, vibrant neighbourhoods full of cafés, galleries, and street art.We visited most of the iconic landmarks, but what I remember most fondly is just wandering without a plan — getting lost in cobbled streets, having tea in tiny cafés, talking to locals. The food was also extraordinary.The reason I would love to go back is that I feel I only scratched the surface on my first visit. Istanbul is one of those cities that gets under your skin — you leave feeling like part of you is still there.

part3_questions.question: What's the difference between the city and the countryside?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think the most obvious difference is the pace of life — cities tend to be fast-moving and demanding, while the countryside offers a slower, more deliberate rhythm. Beyond that, access to opportunities is very different — cities typically offer far more in terms of education and employment. That said, the countryside has its own profound advantages — cleaner air, stronger community bonds, and a sense of space that city living can rarely replicate.

part3_questions.question: Do you think people in the countryside are friendlier than people in cities?
part3_questions.model_answer: It's a common generalisation, and honestly, I think it has some basis in reality — in smaller communities, people tend to know their neighbours and look out for each other. But I would not say city people are unfriendly — they are often just more pressed for time and less accustomed to stopping for conversation. I've experienced genuine warmth in both settings, so I think it really comes down to the individual.

part3_questions.question: Some people say large cities are suitable for old people. What do you think?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think it really depends on the city and the person. Large cities can actually be incredibly well-suited for older people — they often have better healthcare facilities, public transport, and cultural activities. On the other hand, the noise, pace, and cost of living can be very challenging. Personally, I think what matters most is social connection — wherever older people feel connected to a community, that is where they thrive.

part3_questions.question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of tourism?
part3_questions.model_answer: On the positive side, tourism brings significant economic benefits — it creates jobs and generates revenue for local economies. It also promotes cultural exchange in a way that can deepen mutual understanding. However, overtourism can put enormous pressure on local infrastructure and dilute the authenticity of a place. So I think the goal should be sustainable, responsible tourism.

part3_questions.question: Do tourists prefer to visit modern cities or historic cities?
part3_questions.model_answer: From what I've observed, most tourists are actually drawn to places with history and character — old streets, ancient monuments, cultural heritage. That said, many modern cities have also become major tourist destinations because of their architecture and creative energy. I think what people ultimately want is authenticity — a place that feels genuinely distinct, whether that comes from history or contemporary culture.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PERSONDescribe a person who makes plans a lot and is good at planning
bullets: How you knew him / her and what plans he / she makes
And explain how you feel about this person
part2.model_answer: ⏱ Approx. 2 minutes at natural speaking paceThe person who comes to mind immediately is my older sister, Nilufar. She has always been extraordinarily organised — the kind of person who has colour-coded calendars, detailed to-do lists, and somehow manages to stay on top of everything without seeming stressed about it.We grew up together, so I have had a front-row seat to her planning habits all my life. What I remember most from childhood is how she would plan family events months in advance — making checklists, allocating responsibilities, thinking through every possible detail.The kinds of plans she makes range from the everyday to the very long-term. On a day-to-day basis she plans her week every Sunday evening. But she also plans on a much larger scale — she started saving and planning for her apartment four years before she actually bought it.As for how I feel about her, I have enormous admiration for her discipline and foresight. Watching her navigate major life events with such calm and precision has genuinely changed how I approach my own planning.

part3_questions.question: Do you think it is important to plan ahead?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, absolutely — at least to some extent. Planning gives you a sense of direction and helps you use your time and resources more effectively. That said, I think there is a balance to strike — over-planning can sometimes leave you rigid and inflexible when things change. The ideal is to have a clear general direction while staying open to adapting as circumstances evolve.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people not like making plans?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think it comes down to a few different reasons. Some people find planning anxiety-inducing — committing to a plan makes them feel trapped or scared of failure. Others genuinely thrive on spontaneity and feel that planning takes the joy out of things. And then there are those who simply haven't developed the habit, not because they dislike it, but because they've never been taught how to do it effectively.

part3_questions.question: Do you think planning skills are more important today than in the past?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think so, yes. The pace and complexity of modern life means there is simply more to manage — more information, more choices, more competing demands on our time. In the past, life was often more structured by tradition and routine, so less explicit planning was needed. Today, the ability to prioritise, organise, and think ahead is arguably one of the most valuable skills a person can have.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PERSONDescribe a person who solved a problem in a smart way
bullets: Who this person is and what the problem was
And explain why you think he / she did it in a smart way
part2.model_answer: ⏱ Approx. 2 minutes at natural speaking paceThe person I want to talk about is a close friend of mine named Jasur — someone I have known since university, and someone whose remarkable ability to think outside the box when faced with a difficult situation has always impressed me.The problem I am thinking of happened about two years ago. Jasur was working on a small business project with some friends, and they ran into a serious cash-flow problem just weeks before a crucial deadline. Most of us would have panicked or given up, but Jasur instead sat down with the team, mapped out every unnecessary expense, and then came up with a creative arrangement with one of their suppliers — offering them a stake in future profits in exchange for extended payment terms. It was a win-win solution that nobody else had thought of.What made it genuinely smart, in my opinion, was not just the solution itself but how he arrived at it. He remained completely calm under pressure, asked the right questions, and looked at the problem from multiple angles before settling on an approach.Looking back, I think that experience taught me something important about the difference between intelligence and wisdom. Jasur is not necessarily the most academically brilliant person I know, but he has an extraordinary ability to stay composed and find creative, practical solutions. That, I think is a genuinely rare and valuable quality.

part3_questions.question: How do children become smart at school?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think it is less about raw intelligence and more about developing the right habits and mindset. Children who learn how to ask good questions, stay curious, and engage actively with material tend to do far better than those who simply memorise content passively. Beyond that, good teachers play an enormous role — when a teacher makes learning feel relevant and exciting, children naturally invest far more effort. So I think teaching quality and environment are arguably just as important as innate ability.

part3_questions.question: Are clever children happier than other children?
part3_questions.model_answer: Not necessarily — and I think it is actually a dangerous assumption to make. Intelligence can sometimes be isolating, particularly if a child feels different from their peers or faces excessive academic pressure. What tends to make children genuinely happy is feeling connected, valued, and confident — not a particular level of academic achievement. I'd argue that the two do not automatically go hand in hand.

part3_questions.question: Do you think children are born smart, or do they learn to become smart?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think it is clearly a combination of both — the classic nature versus nurture debate. Children are born with different cognitive capacities and learning styles, which are partly genetic. But the research on neuroplasticity strongly suggests that intelligence is also something that can be actively developed through the right experiences and effort. I would argue that mindset matters enormously — children who believe they can improve tend to do exactly that, while those who see intelligence as fixed often stop trying when things get hard.

part2.topic: PART 2 — OBJECTDescribe a piece of technology (not a phone) that you would like to own
bullets: How much it costs and what you will use it for
And explain why you would like to own it

It would also allow me to develop a skill set that could be professionally useful as well as personally fulfilling. Honestly, it is the kind of purchase I could justify from every angle, which is what makes it feel like a worthwhile investment rather than just an indulgence.

part3_questions.question: What kinds of technology do young people like to use?
part3_questions.model_answer: From what I can observe, young people are primarily drawn to mobile-first technology — smartphones, wireless earbuds, and streaming platforms. Social media apps are an enormous part of daily life for most people my age. Beyond that, there has been a growing interest in wearable technology. What is interesting is that young people adopt new technology very quickly — there is much less resistance to change compared to older generations.

part3_questions.question: What are the differences between the technology of the past and that of today?
part3_questions.model_answer: The most fundamental shift is probably connectivity — technology today is almost entirely defined by its ability to link people and information. In the past, devices were largely standalone and single-purpose. A calculator just calculated; a camera just took photographs. Today, a single device handles communication, navigation, photography, and entertainment simultaneously. The other major difference is accessibility — technology that was once available only to institutions or the very wealthy is now widely affordable.

part3_questions.question: Do you think wearable technology like smart watches is useful?
part3_questions.model_answer: Genuinely, yes — I think wearable technology has moved well beyond being a novelty. For people who are serious about their health and fitness, smartwatches provide real-time data that can genuinely change behaviour — tracking heart rate, sleep quality, and activity levels. My one reservation is around privacy — the amount of personal biometric data these devices collect is significant.

part3_questions.question: What are the benefits of technology for people?
part3_questions.model_answer: The benefits are enormous and genuinely transformative. Technology has made access to information, education, and healthcare far more equitable. It has also dramatically improved productivity and communication, allowing people to collaborate across geographic boundaries in ways that were inconceivable even twenty years ago. On a more personal level, it connects people to communities and support networks that might not exist in their immediate physical environment.

part3_questions.question: Should children be allowed to use technology?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, I think so — but with clear boundaries and guidance. Technology is so deeply embedded in modern life that preventing children from engaging with it entirely would leave them genuinely unprepared for adulthood. The key is ensuring that technology use is age-appropriate, balanced with offline activities, and that children are developing the critical thinking skills to navigate digital spaces safely. The problem is not technology itself but unregulated, passive consumption without educational value.

part3_questions.question: How can online communication improve family relationships?
part3_questions.model_answer: For families that are geographically separated, online communication has been genuinely transformative — it allows people to maintain close relationships across continents in a way that simply was not possible before. Video calls in particular have made a huge difference, allowing grandparents to watch their grandchildren grow up even from the other side of the world. I think for many families, these tools have actually strengthened relationships that physical distance might otherwise have eroded.

part3_questions.question: How has technology changed the way people communicate?
part3_questions.model_answer: Fundamentally and in almost every dimension. Communication is now instant, constant, and primarily text-based, which has both advantages and disadvantages. We can reach anyone anywhere within seconds, which is remarkable. But the shift away from voice and face-to-face interaction has meant that nuance, emotion, and depth is sometimes lost. I think most people would acknowledge that written messages, however convenient, rarely convey the same richness as an actual conversation.

part3_questions.question: What are the differences between online and face-to-face communication?
part3_questions.model_answer: The most significant difference is the presence of non-verbal cues — in face-to-face communication, body language, tone of voice, and facial expressions carry an enormous amount of meaning that is simply absent in text-based exchanges. This makes online communication more prone to misunderstanding. On the other hand, online communication gives people more time to think before they respond, which can lead to more considered and well-articulated exchanges. Both have their strengths depending on the context.

part3_questions.question: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think it is fair to say yes, in some respects. The level of cognitive offloading we do to technology — relying on GPS rather than learning routes, using calculators for basic arithmetic, letting algorithms decide what we read — is genuinely significant. I'm not sure this is entirely negative, since these tools free up mental resources for more complex tasks. But I do think that in areas like sustained attention and deep thinking, our over-reliance is causing real problems.

part3_questions.question: What negative effects does technology have on people's relationships?
part3_questions.model_answer: Probably the most significant is the erosion of quality attention — being physically present with someone but mentally somewhere else, distracted by a screen. Technology also makes it easier to avoid difficult conversations by retreating into digital communication, which can prevent the honest, vulnerable exchanges that strong relationships actually need. And at a broader level, social media has introduced a culture of comparison and performance that is genuinely damaging to how people feel about their lives.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PERSONDescribe a famous person you would like to meet
bullets: Why you would like to meet them
And explain what you would talk about if you met them
part2.model_answer: The person I would most like to meet is Malala Yousafzai. She is a Pakistani education activist who became the youngest ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate. I have followed her story since she survived a terrible attack simply for advocating girls' education. What I find most inspiring is not just her courage, but her refusal to become bitter or vengeful. If I met her, I would want to ask how she maintains hope and optimism in the face of such darkness. I think her answer would change how I see my own challenges.

part3_questions.question: What kinds of people become famous in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: In Uzbekistan, singers, actors, and sportspeople tend to dominate the celebrity landscape. In recent years, social media influencers have also risen to prominence, particularly among younger audiences. Politicians and business leaders are also well-known, though they tend to be respected rather than adored.

part3_questions.question: Do you think celebrities have a responsibility to be good role models?
part3_questions.model_answer: To some extent, yes. When someone has a platform that reaches millions, their behaviour inevitably influences others — particularly young people. That said, celebrities are human beings with flaws like anyone else, and holding them to an impossible standard is neither fair nor realistic. I think the responsibility lies more in being honest about their imperfections rather than pretending to be perfect.

part3_questions.question: Is it better to be famous for talent or for personality?
part3_questions.model_answer: I would argue talent has more lasting value. Personality-driven fame often depends on novelty and controversy, which can fade quickly. Talent, on the other hand, tends to build a more enduring legacy. But ideally, the two go together — someone who is both genuinely skilled and authentically themselves.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people want to be famous?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think the desire for recognition and validation is deeply human. Fame promises attention, admiration, and a sense of significance. For some, it is also about influence — the ability to shape conversations and causes they care about. However, I think many people underestimate the costs of fame — loss of privacy, constant scrutiny, and the pressure to maintain a public image.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PERSONDescribe a historical figure you admire
bullets: And explain what we can learn from them today
part2.model_answer: The historical figure I most admire is Amir Timur, also known as Tamerlane. He was a Central Asian conqueror and statesman who founded the Timurid Empire in the fourteenth century. What impresses me most is not just his military genius, but his extraordinary vision for culture and architecture. He commissioned some of the most beautiful buildings in Central Asia, many of which still stand today. I think we can learn from his ability to combine strength with a deep appreciation for art and knowledge. In an age of conflict, his example reminds us that power and culture can coexist.

part3_questions.question: Do you think it is important to learn about history?
part3_questions.model_answer: Absolutely. History is not just a record of the past — it is a laboratory of human behaviour. Understanding how societies have risen and fallen helps us recognise patterns in our own time. Without historical knowledge, we are vulnerable to repeating the same mistakes.

part3_questions.question: How do people learn about history in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: Primarily through school, but also through museums, monuments, and family stories. In Uzbekistan, history is very much alive in the architecture of our cities — Samarkand and Bukhara are essentially open-air history museums. Television documentaries and films also play an important role.

part3_questions.question: Are historical films accurate?
part3_questions.model_answer: Rarely completely. Filmmakers inevitably simplify, dramatise, and sometimes invent events for narrative purposes. That does not make them worthless — they can spark genuine interest in history — but viewers should approach them critically and seek out scholarly sources for the full picture.

part3_questions.question: Should governments spend money preserving historical sites?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, without question. Historical sites are irreplaceable links to our shared past. They attract tourism, create jobs, and foster a sense of national identity. The cost of preservation is far lower than the cost of losing something that can never be recreated.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PERSONDescribe a teacher who has influenced you
bullets: And explain what you learned from them
part2.model_answer: The teacher who had the deepest influence on me was my secondary school mathematics teacher, Mr Karimov. At first, I found maths intimidating and dry. But he had an extraordinary gift for making abstract concepts feel concrete and relevant — he would use real-world examples from architecture, economics, and even music to show why equations mattered. What I learned from him was not just mathematics, but a way of thinking. He taught me that every problem can be broken down into smaller, solvable pieces. That mindset has served me in every area of my life, not just academics.

part3_questions.question: What qualities make a good teacher?
part3_questions.model_answer: Passion for the subject, genuine care for students, and the ability to explain complex ideas clearly. A good teacher also adapts to different learning styles and creates an environment where students feel safe to ask questions and make mistakes.

part3_questions.question: Do you think teachers are underpaid?
part3_questions.model_answer: In many countries, yes. Teaching is one of the most important professions in society, yet it is rarely compensated at a level that reflects its value. Low salaries can discourage talented people from entering the profession, which ultimately harms students and society as a whole.

part3_questions.question: How has teaching changed in recent years?
part3_questions.model_answer: Technology has transformed the classroom. Interactive whiteboards, online resources, and remote learning have expanded what is possible. However, the fundamental relationship between teacher and student remains unchanged. The best technology enhances good teaching but cannot replace it.

part3_questions.question: Should teachers be strict or friendly?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think the ideal is a balance — firm but fair, warm but not permissive. Students need structure and high expectations to grow, but they also need to feel that their teacher genuinely cares about them. Striking that balance is what separates good teachers from great ones.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PERSONDescribe a friend who is a good listener
bullets: Why you think they are a good listener
And explain how they help you
part2.model_answer: The person who comes to mind is my closest friend, Dilnoza. We met at university during a group project and quickly discovered that we shared similar values. What makes her such an exceptional listener is that she does not simply wait for her turn to speak — she genuinely absorbs what you are saying, asks thoughtful follow-up questions, and remembers details from previous conversations. When I am going through something difficult, talking to her does not just make me feel heard — it helps me understand my own feelings more clearly. She has a rare gift for making people feel safe and accepted.

part3_questions.question: Do you think listening is an important skill?
part3_questions.model_answer: Absolutely — and one that is surprisingly rare. Most people listen only long enough to formulate their own response. Genuine listening requires patience, empathy, and the willingness to be changed by what you hear. In both personal and professional relationships, it is one of the most valuable skills you can cultivate.

part3_questions.question: Are people good listeners nowadays?
part3_questions.model_answer: Honestly, I think the constant presence of smartphones has eroded our collective listening capacity. People are often physically present but mentally elsewhere. Deep, undistracted conversation feels increasingly like a luxury rather than a norm.

part3_questions.question: How can someone become a better listener?
part3_questions.model_answer: Put away your phone, make eye contact, and resist the urge to interrupt or offer solutions immediately. Ask open-ended questions that show you are genuinely curious. And perhaps most importantly, be comfortable with silence — sometimes people need a moment to gather their thoughts.

part3_questions.question: Do men or women tend to be better listeners?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think it varies far more by individual than by gender. Cultural stereotypes suggest women are more emotionally attuned, but I have met men who are extraordinarily perceptive listeners and women who are not. Personality, upbringing, and intention matter far more than gender.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACEDescribe a place you would like to visit in the future
bullets: Why you want to go there
And explain why you haven't gone yet
part2.model_answer: The place I most want to visit is Japan — specifically Kyoto during cherry blossom season. I have been fascinated by Japanese culture for years — the blend of ancient tradition and cutting-edge modernity, the emphasis on craftsmanship and attention to detail. In Kyoto, I would visit the historic temples and gardens, try authentic kaiseki cuisine, and simply wander the narrow streets of the old city. I have not gone yet because it requires significant time and money, and I want to do it properly rather than rushing through in a few days. I am saving up and planning to go next spring.

part3_questions.question: What kinds of places do tourists usually visit?
part3_questions.model_answer: It varies by traveller, but most people gravitate towards famous landmarks, natural wonders, and culturally significant sites. Cities with good food and nightlife are also extremely popular. Increasingly, people seek authentic, off-the-beaten-path experiences rather than purely touristy ones.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people prefer to travel abroad rather than in their own country?
part3_questions.model_answer: Curiosity about the unfamiliar is a powerful motivator. Foreign travel offers new languages, cuisines, and ways of life that can be genuinely transformative. Domestic travel, while wonderful, sometimes lacks that sense of discovery. That said, I think many people underestimate how much their own country has to offer.

part3_questions.question: Do you think international travel is good for the economy?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, very much so. Tourism creates jobs, supports local businesses, and generates tax revenue. However, the benefits are not always evenly distributed — large hotel chains and tour operators often capture more of the profit than local communities. Sustainable tourism models are needed.

part3_questions.question: What are the disadvantages of mass tourism?
part3_questions.model_answer: Overtourism can degrade the very attractions that draw visitors — ancient monuments wear down, natural habitats are damaged, and local residents are priced out of their own neighbourhoods. It can also create a kind of cultural Disneyland where authenticity is replaced by performance.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACEDescribe a beautiful place in your country
bullets: And explain why you think it is beautiful
part2.model_answer: The place I want to describe is the Charvak Reservoir, located about an hour's drive from Tashkent in the mountains. It is an enormous artificial lake surrounded by dramatic rocky peaks that change colour throughout the day — from deep blue-grey in the morning to warm amber at sunset. In summer, the water is a striking turquoise, and people come to swim, boat, and hike the surrounding trails. What makes it truly beautiful, in my opinion, is the contrast between the stillness of the water and the ruggedness of the mountains. It feels like a place where nature has the upper hand, and that humility is refreshing.

part3_questions.question: Do you think natural beauty is important?
part3_questions.model_answer: Absolutely — and not just aesthetically. Exposure to natural beauty has measurable effects on mental health, reducing stress and improving mood. It also reminds us of something larger than ourselves, which is a valuable antidote to the self-absorption that modern life often encourages.

part3_questions.question: Should governments protect natural landscapes?
part3_questions.model_answer: Without question. Natural landscapes are public goods that belong to everyone, including future generations. Once destroyed, they cannot be recreated. Governments have both the authority and the obligation to protect them through national parks, conservation laws, and sustainable development policies.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people prefer cities to the countryside?
part3_questions.model_answer: Cities offer convenience, opportunity, and stimulation. For people who thrive on energy and variety, rural life can feel isolating and dull. The countryside, while beautiful, does not offer the same career prospects, cultural amenities, or social density that many people value.

part3_questions.question: Do you think technology has made it harder to appreciate nature?
part3_questions.model_answer: In some ways, yes. Screens compete for our attention, and the instant gratification of digital content can make the slow, subtle rewards of nature feel boring by comparison. But technology can also connect people to nature — through nature documentaries, photography, and apps that identify plants and stars.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACEDescribe a city you have visited
bullets: And explain why you liked or disliked it
part2.model_answer: The city I want to talk about is Seoul, which I visited two years ago. I spent about ten days there, staying in a small guesthouse in the Hongdae district. During the day, I explored ancient palaces like Gyeongbokgung, wandered through the Bukchon Hanok Village, and visited several museums. In the evenings, I sampled street food at the night markets and soaked in the energy of the city. What I loved most was the seamless blend of old and new — you can walk from a five-hundred-year-old palace to a futuristic shopping mall in minutes. The people were also incredibly polite and helpful, even when there was a language barrier.

part3_questions.question: What makes a city attractive to tourists?
part3_questions.model_answer: A combination of unique attractions, good infrastructure, and a welcoming atmosphere. Tourists want to see things they cannot see at home — historic sites, distinctive architecture, local cuisine. But they also need reliable transport, safe streets, and friendly locals to have a positive experience.

part3_questions.question: Do you think cities are becoming too similar?
part3_questions.model_answer: In some respects, yes. Global chains and shopping malls can make one city feel interchangeable with another. However, I think the truly distinctive character of a city — its history, its people, its food culture — is harder to homogenise. The challenge for modern cities is to develop without losing their soul.

part3_questions.question: What problems do big cities face?
part3_questions.model_answer: Traffic congestion, air pollution, housing affordability, and social inequality are the most pressing. As cities grow, these problems tend to compound. Effective urban planning — good public transport, green spaces, and mixed-income housing — is essential but often politically difficult to implement.

part3_questions.question: Should people live in cities or in the countryside?
part3_questions.model_answer: It depends entirely on individual priorities. Cities offer career opportunities, culture, and convenience. The countryside offers space, quiet, and a slower pace. I do not think there is a universal answer — what matters is that people have genuine choice.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACEDescribe your favourite restaurant
bullets: What kind of food it serves
And explain how often you go there
part2.model_answer: My favourite restaurant is a small family-run place called Anor, located in a quiet corner of the old city. They specialise in traditional Uzbek cuisine — plov, manti, shashlik — but with a level of care and attention that sets them apart. The ingredients are incredibly fresh, the portions are generous, and the flavours are authentic without being heavy. But what really makes it special is the atmosphere. The owner often comes out to chat with guests, and there is a genuine warmth that you cannot fake. I go there perhaps once a month, usually with family or close friends, and it never disappoints.

part3_questions.question: Do people in your country eat out often?
part3_questions.model_answer: More often than in the past, particularly in cities. Dining out has become a regular social activity rather than a rare treat. However, home-cooked meals still hold a central place in family life, especially for special occasions and family gatherings.

part3_questions.question: What is the difference between fast food and traditional food?
part3_questions.model_answer: Fast food prioritises speed, consistency, and cost over quality and nutrition. Traditional food is usually prepared with fresh, local ingredients using recipes passed down through generations. It takes longer to make but tends to be healthier and more flavourful.

part3_questions.question: Why do some restaurants succeed while others fail?
part3_questions.model_answer: Successful restaurants consistently deliver good food, good service, and good atmosphere. Location matters enormously, as does effective marketing. But above all, word of mouth is decisive — people return to places where they feel genuinely welcomed and well-fed.

part3_questions.question: Do you think cooking shows are popular?
part3_questions.model_answer: Very much so. They have turned cooking into a form of entertainment and elevated chefs to celebrity status. While some people actually cook what they see, many simply watch for the pleasure of it — the beautiful plating, the drama of competition, and the vicarious satisfaction of a well-prepared meal.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACEDescribe an important building in your city
bullets: And explain why it is important
part2.model_answer: The building I want to describe is the Amir Timur Museum in Tashkent. It is an impressive, modern building with a striking blue dome, located right in the centre of the city. Inside, it houses a rich collection of artefacts, manuscripts, and artworks from the Timurid period. But its importance goes beyond what is inside. The museum stands as a powerful symbol of national identity and historical pride. For visitors, it offers an accessible introduction to the depth and sophistication of Central Asian civilisation. For locals, it is a reminder of a glorious past and an inspiration for the future.

part3_questions.question: What kinds of buildings are important in a city?
part3_questions.model_answer: Public buildings that serve collective needs — museums, libraries, transport hubs, parks. But I also think ordinary residential architecture matters enormously because it shapes how people experience daily life. A city with beautiful, well-maintained public spaces feels fundamentally different from one that neglects them.

part3_questions.question: Should old buildings be preserved or demolished?
part3_questions.model_answer: Preserved, wherever possible. Old buildings carry history, craftsmanship, and a sense of place that new buildings rarely replicate. Demolition should be a last resort, reserved for buildings that are genuinely unsafe or no longer fit for purpose. Adaptive reuse — converting old buildings for modern needs — is usually the best solution.

part3_questions.question: Do you think architecture affects people's mood?
part3_questions.model_answer: Definitely. Studies consistently show that people feel better in spaces with natural light, greenery, and human-scale design. Overly concrete, poorly lit environments can contribute to stress and anxiety. Good architecture is not just functional — it is psychological.

part3_questions.question: What is the most important building in your opinion?
part3_questions.model_answer: If I had to choose, I would say the library — particularly a well-designed public library. It is one of the few buildings that exists purely to democratise knowledge and create a space for learning, regardless of income. A good library is a genuine public good.

part2.topic: PART 2 — PLACEDescribe a park or garden you enjoy
bullets: And explain why you enjoy it
part2.model_answer: The park I want to talk about is Alisher Navoi National Park, which is not far from where I live. It is a large, well-maintained space with tree-lined paths, open lawns, and a small lake where people rent paddle boats in summer. I usually go there on weekend mornings for a jog or a walk, and sometimes I bring a book and sit on one of the benches. What I love most is the sense of calm it offers — even though it is in the middle of a busy city, the noise fades away once you are inside. It feels like a small sanctuary where I can reset before the week begins.

part3_questions.question: Do you think parks are important in cities?
part3_questions.model_answer: Essential. They provide space for exercise, relaxation, and social connection. They also improve air quality, reduce the urban heat island effect, and support biodiversity. A city without adequate green space is simply less liveable.

part3_questions.question: Should parks be free to enter?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, absolutely. Parks are public goods and should be accessible to everyone regardless of income. Charging entry fees would exclude the people who need them most. The cost of maintenance should be borne by the city, not by individual visitors.

part3_questions.question: What activities do people do in parks in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: Walking, jogging, picnicking, playing football, and simply sitting and chatting. In summer, you often see families and groups of friends gathering for barbecues and celebrations. Older people tend to use them for gentle exercise and socialising.

part3_questions.question: Do you think there are enough parks in your city?
part3_questions.model_answer: Not really. While the central parks are lovely, many residential neighbourhoods lack green space. Children in particular need safe places to play, and adults need places to unwind. I think urban planners could do more to integrate small green spaces into every neighbourhood.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a memorable holiday you had
bullets: And explain why it was memorable
part2.model_answer: The most memorable holiday I have had was a trip to the Fergana Valley with my grandparents about three years ago. We stayed in a small village where my grandfather grew up, in a traditional house with a courtyard and an orchard. During the day, we visited local craftsmen — ceramicists, weavers, and bakers — and my grandfather told stories about his childhood. In the evenings, we ate meals cooked by my grandmother and listened to traditional music. What made it unforgettable was the sense of connection — to my family history, to the land, and to a way of life that is slowly disappearing. It was not luxurious, but it was profoundly meaningful.

part3_questions.question: Why do people go on holiday?
part3_questions.model_answer: To break from routine, recharge mentally, and experience something new. Holidays offer a change of scenery and pace that can be genuinely restorative. They also create shared memories and strengthen relationships with the people you travel with.

part3_questions.question: Do you think holidays have become too commercialised?
part3_questions.model_answer: To some extent, yes. The travel industry has created enormous pressure to consume — luxury hotels, Instagram-worthy destinations, endless souvenirs. But at its core, a holiday does not need to be expensive or glamorous to be valuable. The best holidays are often the simplest ones.

part3_questions.question: What is more important on holiday — relaxation or adventure?
part3_questions.model_answer: It depends on the person and the moment. Sometimes you genuinely need to do absolutely nothing. Other times, you need the stimulation of new experiences. I think the best holidays offer a balance — enough activity to feel alive, and enough rest to actually recover.

part3_questions.question: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3_questions.model_answer: It has become faster, cheaper, and more accessible. Budget airlines and online booking have opened up international travel to far more people. However, it has also become more homogeneous — the same hotel chains, the same shops, the same experiences in every city. Authentic, slow travel is harder to find.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EVENTDescribe a wedding you attended
bullets: And explain what you enjoyed about it
part2.model_answer: The wedding I want to describe was my cousin's, which took place last summer in a beautiful traditional venue on the outskirts of Tashkent. It was a large celebration — probably three hundred guests — and it lasted well into the night. The ceremony itself was deeply moving, with heartfelt speeches and traditional blessings. But what I enjoyed most was the atmosphere of joy and community. People from different generations came together, there was live music and dancing, and the food was extraordinary. Weddings in our culture are not just about the couple — they are a celebration of family, and that collective happiness is infectious.

part3_questions.question: What are weddings like in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: They are typically large, multi-day celebrations with hundreds of guests. There is a religious ceremony, a lavish reception with traditional music and dancing, and often a smaller family gathering the next day. Hospitality is taken very seriously — the hosts feel a deep obligation to ensure every guest is well-fed and entertained.

part3_questions.question: Do you think big weddings are a waste of money?
part3_questions.model_answer: It depends. If the couple is going into serious debt for a single day, then yes, it is unwise. But if they can afford it and it brings genuine joy to their families, then it is not wasted money — it is an investment in memory and connection. The problem is when social pressure overrides personal preference.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people prefer to get married abroad?
part3_questions.model_answer: For the scenery, the romance, and sometimes to escape the expectations and guest list of a traditional home wedding. A destination wedding is usually smaller and more intimate. The downside is that many loved ones may not be able to afford the travel.

part3_questions.question: Has the concept of marriage changed in recent years?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, significantly. People are marrying later, if at all, and there is far greater acceptance of different kinds of partnerships. Gender roles within marriage have also shifted, with more shared responsibility for childcare and household tasks. The institution is evolving to reflect modern values.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EVENTDescribe a concert or music event you enjoyed
bullets: Where and when it took place
And explain why you enjoyed it
part2.model_answer: The concert that stands out in my memory was a live performance by a traditional Uzbek music ensemble at the State Conservatory about a year ago. I went with my parents, who have always loved classical and folk music. The concert featured a range of instruments — the dutar, the doira, and the rubab — played with extraordinary skill and passion. What made it special was the sense of cultural pride in the room. Between pieces, the musicians explained the history of each composition, and you could feel the audience's deep connection to the music. It was not just entertainment — it was a reminder of who we are.

part3_questions.question: What kinds of music are popular in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: Pop, hip-hop, and electronic music dominate among young people. But traditional folk music and classical maqom also have devoted audiences, particularly among older generations. There has also been a revival of interest in traditional instruments among young musicians, which is encouraging.

part3_questions.question: Do you think live music is better than recorded music?
part3_questions.model_answer: They serve different purposes. Live music has an energy and spontaneity that recordings cannot capture — the interaction between performers and audience creates something unique each time. But recorded music offers perfect fidelity, convenience, and the ability to revisit favourite performances endlessly.

part3_questions.question: Should governments support the arts?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, absolutely. The arts enrich public life, preserve cultural heritage, and foster creativity across all sectors. Without public support, many forms of art would become economically unviable and accessible only to the wealthy. A society that neglects the arts is a poorer society in every sense.

part3_questions.question: Why do young people like going to concerts?
part3_questions.model_answer: For the shared experience and the sense of belonging. A concert is a space where you can be completely immersed in something you love, surrounded by people who feel the same way. It is also a break from the curated, filtered world of social media — it is raw, immediate, and real.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EVENTDescribe a sports event you watched
bullets: And explain why you enjoyed it
part2.model_answer: The sports event I want to talk about was the AFC Asian Cup qualifier match between Uzbekistan and South Korea, which I watched at the Milliy Stadium in Tashkent. I went with a group of university friends, and the atmosphere was electric from the moment we arrived. The stadium was packed with fans wearing national colours, waving flags, and singing traditional chants. Uzbekistan played with incredible determination, and although the match ended in a draw, the quality of the game was superb. What I loved most was the collective emotion — thousands of strangers united by hope and pride. It was far more powerful than watching on television.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people enjoy watching sports more than playing them?
part3_questions.model_answer: Watching allows you to experience the drama and skill without the physical demands. It is also a social activity — you share the emotional highs and lows with fellow fans. For some, the tactical and analytical side of sport is genuinely fascinating in its own right.

part3_questions.question: Do you think sports bring people together?
part3_questions.model_answer: Absolutely. There is something uniquely unifying about cheering for the same team or celebrating a shared victory. Sport transcends language, politics, and social divisions in a way that few other things can. At its best, it creates a sense of community and collective identity.

part3_questions.question: Should governments invest in sports facilities?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, very much so. Accessible, well-maintained facilities encourage physical activity, which improves public health and reduces healthcare costs in the long run. They also create opportunities for young people to develop discipline, teamwork, and resilience.

part3_questions.question: What are the disadvantages of professional sports?
part3_questions.model_answer: The pressure on athletes can be immense, often leading to injuries, mental health struggles, and burnout. There is also a commercial side that can feel exploitative — the enormous salaries of top players while grassroots sports remain underfunded. And in some countries, nationalism around sport can become toxic and divisive.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a time you helped someone
bullets: And explain how you felt about it
part2.model_answer: The time that comes to mind was about six months ago when a classmate of mine was struggling terribly with a programming assignment. She was on the verge of tears because the deadline was the next day and nothing she tried was working. I spent about three hours with her, walking through the logic step by step, helping her debug her code, and reassuring her that she was capable of doing it. By the end, she had not only finished the assignment but actually understood the concepts behind it. What made me feel genuinely good was not just the act of helping, but seeing her confidence grow. It reminded me that sometimes people just need someone to believe in them.

part3_questions.question: Do you think people help others enough?
part3_questions.model_answer: I think most people are willing to help when asked directly, but we are often so absorbed in our own lives that we do not notice when others are struggling. A culture of individualism and busyness makes spontaneous acts of kindness less common than they should be.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people refuse to help others?
part3_questions.model_answer: Sometimes it is fear — fear of being taken advantage of, fear of getting involved in something complicated, or simply not having the time or energy. In some cultures, there is also a strong emphasis on self-reliance, which can make offering or accepting help feel like an admission of weakness.

part3_questions.question: Should schools teach children to help others?
part3_questions.model_answer: Absolutely. Altruism and empathy are partly innate, but they are also skills that can be cultivated. Schools that encourage cooperation, community service, and mentoring create young people who are not just academically capable but socially responsible.

part3_questions.question: What is more important — helping family or strangers?
part3_questions.model_answer: Both matter, but I think family usually comes first because the bond is deeper and the obligation more personal. That said, helping a stranger often requires a more conscious, deliberate choice, which can make it feel more meaningful in a different way.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a time you received good news
bullets: When and where you heard it
And explain how you felt about it
part2.model_answer: The good news I remember most vividly was finding out that I had been accepted into my preferred university programme. I had worked towards it for years, and the application process had been intensely competitive. I was at home when the email arrived, and I remember my hands actually shaking as I opened it. When I read the words 'We are pleased to offer you a place,' I felt a wave of relief and joy that is genuinely hard to describe. I immediately called my parents, and we celebrated with a special dinner that evening. What made it so meaningful was not just the achievement itself, but the validation that all the hard work had been worth it.

part3_questions.question: How do people share good news in your country?
part3_questions.model_answer: In person, if possible — visiting someone's home or inviting them for a meal. Phone calls are common for immediate family, while social media announcements are increasingly popular for wider circles. The method usually reflects the significance of the news and the closeness of the relationship.

part3_questions.question: Do you think good news spreads faster than bad news?
part3_questions.model_answer: Bad news usually spreads faster because it triggers stronger emotional reactions and a sense of urgency. Good news tends to travel more slowly unless it is truly extraordinary. However, social media has changed this dynamic somewhat — viral good news stories can spread incredibly quickly.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people prefer to keep good news private?
part3_questions.model_answer: Fear of envy, a desire to avoid pressure or expectations, or simply a private nature. Some people also worry that sharing good news might make others feel bad about their own situations. I think there is a certain wisdom in keeping some things sacred.

part3_questions.question: Is it important to celebrate achievements?
part3_questions.model_answer: Yes, very much. Celebration marks a milestone, creates a memory, and allows others to share in your joy. It also provides a moment of reflection before moving on to the next challenge. Life moves quickly, and without celebration, achievements can feel hollow and quickly forgotten.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a time you were late for something important
bullets: And explain how you felt about it
part2.model_answer: The time I was late that really sticks in my memory was an important job interview about two years ago. I had allowed plenty of time, but an unexpected road closure caused a traffic jam that lasted nearly an hour. I arrived twenty minutes late, flustered and apologetic. To my relief, the interviewer was understanding, and the interview went reasonably well. However, I could not shake the feeling that I had made a poor first impression. It taught me a valuable lesson: always have a backup plan and leave far more time than you think you need. Being late for something important is one of the most stressful experiences imaginable.

part3_questions.question: Why are some people always late?
part3_questions.model_answer: Often it is poor time management or a tendency to underestimate how long tasks take. Some people are also easily distracted or struggle with transitions. In a few cases, chronic lateness can be a form of passive resistance or a way of asserting control.

part3_questions.question: Is punctuality important in your culture?
part3_questions.model_answer: It is valued, particularly in professional and formal settings. However, social events tend to be more flexible — arriving slightly late to a party is often expected and even polite. I think the key is knowing which contexts demand strict punctuality and which allow more leeway.

part3_questions.question: How does lateness affect relationships?
part3_questions.model_answer: Repeated lateness can erode trust and make people feel disrespected. It sends a message that your time is more valuable than theirs. However, occasional lateness is usually forgiven if the person is apologetic and communicates properly.

part3_questions.question: What can people do to be more punctual?
part3_questions.model_answer: Build in buffer time, set multiple alarms, prepare the night before, and be honest with yourself about how long things actually take. It also helps to shift your mindset: aim to arrive early rather than exactly on time, and treat other people's time as precious.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a time you made a difficult decision
bullets: And explain how you felt after making it
part2.model_answer: The most difficult decision I have made was choosing to switch my university major from engineering to economics at the end of my first year. It was difficult because I had already invested a year of work, my family had certain expectations, and I was genuinely unsure whether I was making a rational choice or simply avoiding hard work. I spent weeks weighing the options — speaking to professors, researching career prospects, and trying to imagine myself in each field five years down the line. In the end, I chose economics because it aligned more closely with my interests in policy and human behaviour. The moment I submitted the paperwork, I felt a mixture of terror and relief. Looking back, it was the right decision, but at the time it felt like jumping off a cliff.

part3_questions.question: Do you think young people face more difficult decisions than in the past?
part3_questions.model_answer: In some ways, yes. The sheer number of choices available — in education, career, and lifestyle — can be paralysing. Previous generations often had more defined paths. On the other hand, they also had fewer freedoms, so the difficulty was different in nature.

part3_questions.question: Who do people usually turn to for advice when making decisions?
part3_questions.model_answer: Family members, close friends, and mentors are the most common sources. Some people also consult professionals — career counsellors, financial advisors, or therapists. The best advice usually comes from someone who knows you well but is not too emotionally invested in the outcome.

part3_questions.question: Do you think it is better to make decisions quickly or slowly?
part3_questions.model_answer: It depends on the stakes. For low-stakes decisions, speed prevents overthinking and regret. For major life decisions, deliberation is essential. The key is recognising which category a decision falls into and not letting inertia make the choice for you.

part3_questions.question: What are the consequences of making bad decisions?
part3_questions.model_answer: They range from minor inconvenience to life-altering setbacks. However, I think the fear of bad decisions is often worse than the reality. Most bad decisions are reversible or adaptable, and they often teach us more than good ones. The real danger is indecision, which can waste years of potential.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a time you lost something important
bullets: What you did to find it
And explain how you felt about it
part2.model_answer: The most important thing I ever lost was my grandmother's gold bracelet, which she had given me on my eighteenth birthday. It was not particularly valuable in monetary terms, but it carried enormous sentimental weight. I lost it during a trip to the mountains — I think it slipped off while I was helping a friend set up a tent. I searched everywhere, retraced my steps, and even asked local staff to keep an eye out. It never turned up. I felt genuinely heartbroken for weeks — not just because of the object itself, but because it felt like I had failed to take care of something precious that had been entrusted to me. The experience taught me to be more mindful with things that carry emotional significance.

part3_questions.question: What do people usually do when they lose something?
part3_questions.model_answer: They retrace their steps, check obvious places, ask people around them, and sometimes post on social media or local lost-and-found groups. For valuable items, they might contact police or insurance companies. The emotional response usually depends on whether the item was replaceable or irreplaceable.

part3_questions.question: Do you think people value material possessions too much?
part3_questions.model_answer: To some extent, yes. Consumer culture encourages us to derive identity and status from what we own. But I also think the problem is not materialism per se, but attachment to things for the wrong reasons. A well-made tool or a meaningful gift can genuinely enrich life.

part3_questions.question: What is more upsetting — losing a valuable item or a sentimental one?
part3_questions.model_answer: A sentimental one, almost always. Valuable items can be replaced with money. Sentimental items are linked to memories, relationships, and identity. Losing them feels like losing a piece of your own history.

part3_questions.question: How can people avoid losing things?
part3_questions.model_answer: Develop simple habits — always putting keys in the same place, using tracking devices for valuables, and doing a quick check before leaving anywhere. Mindfulness also helps — being present rather than distracted reduces carelessness enormously.

part2.topic: PART 2 — EXPERIENCEDescribe a time you got lost
bullets: What you did to find your way
And explain how you felt about it
part2.model_answer: The time I got lost happened in Istanbul, a city whose streets seem designed to confuse even the most careful navigator. I was exploring the backstreets of the old city alone, taking photos and not paying close attention to where I was going. Within half an hour, I realised I had no idea how to get back to my hotel. My phone battery was low, and I did not have a paper map. I ended up asking a local shopkeeper for directions, who not only pointed the way but insisted on walking with me for ten minutes to make sure I found the right street. I felt a mixture of embarrassment and gratitude. It was a humbling reminder that independence has its limits, and that most people are kinder than we expect.

part3_questions.question: Why do some people get lost more easily than others?
part3_questions.model_answer: Some people have a naturally stronger sense of direction and spatial memory. Others are more easily distracted or less observant of their surroundings. Technology has also made us complacent — relying on GPS can erode the natural navigational skills we might otherwise develop.

part3_questions.question: Is it a good idea to travel without a map?
part3_questions.model_answer: In familiar or safe areas, getting deliberately lost can lead to wonderful discoveries. In unfamiliar or remote places, it is risky. I think the best approach is to have a map or GPS available but not to be enslaved by it — use it as a safety net, not a crutch.

part3_questions.question: How has technology changed navigation?
part3_questions.model_answer: It has made getting lost almost obsolete. GPS, Google Maps, and translation apps have removed much of the uncertainty from travel. The downside is that we no longer develop the same spatial awareness and problem-solving skills that previous generations had. We sacrifice serendipity for security.

part3_questions.question: What skills are useful when you are lost?
part3_questions.model_answer: Staying calm, observing landmarks, asking for help, and having basic communication skills in the local language. Resourcefulness and patience are far more valuable than pride. Being lost is not a sign of failure — it is an opportunity to learn.
